sections.title: Flexible cords and cables — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 400 covers flexible cords and flexible cables — the connections between equipment and the building wiring, not wire that is installed as part of the building. It sorts cord types by construction (Table 400.4) and permitted use, and it draws a hard line against using a cord as a substitute for permanent wiring. If the wire is meant to stay in the building, it belongs in a Chapter 3 wiring method, not in a cord.
Uses permitted (400.10) are the ones that need to move or be serviced:
• Pendants
• Portable lamps and portable appliances
• Elevator and hoist cables
• Parts of listed equipment, and similar flexible connections
Uses not permitted (400.12) — a flexible cord may not be:
• (1) Used as a substitute for the fixed wiring of a structure
• (2) Run through holes in walls, structural ceilings, suspended or dropped ceilings, or floors
• (3) Run through doorways, windows, or similar openings
• (4) Attached to building surfaces, except as 368.56(B) and 590.4 permit
• (5) Concealed by walls, floors, or ceilings, or located above suspended or dropped ceilings
• (6) Installed in raceways, except as otherwise permitted in the Code
• (7) Installed where subject to physical damage
The 2020 numbers are 400.10 and 400.12; in the 2017 book the same lists were 400.7 and 400.8.
sections.on_the_job: When you reach for a cord, ask whether the equipment is meant to move, be serviced, or be exchanged. If the answer is no, run a permanent wiring method instead. On a service call at a small Orlando warehouse, Sharma found an air compressor 'temporarily' cord-connected through a hole bored in the wall for over a year, the cord pinched flat where it crossed a doorway. The fix was not a heavier cord: the crew ran a dedicated 20 A branch circuit in EMT to a receptacle beside the compressor — Sharma's commercial minimum — and the cord went back to being the compressor's own short connection. Check the cord jacket marking for the type letter before you trust it in a damp or hard-use location.
sections.why_it_exists: A cord jacket is not a raceway. Building wire gets mechanical protection, support, and a box at every splice; a cord pressed into permanent service gets none of that. Stapled, buried, or pinched in a doorway, its insulation fails quietly — and nobody re-checks it, because everyone assumes the 'temporary' cord was removed years ago.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'use a heavier cord.' A 12 AWG hard-service cord through a wall hole is still a 400.12(2) violation, and an extension cord feeding a fixed appliance is still a substitute for fixed wiring under 400.12(1). Cord size and jacket type never cure a prohibited use.
inspection_fails: Flexible cord run through a hole in a wall, ceiling, or floor to reach fixed equipment (400.12(2)).
Cord passing through a doorway or window opening, pinched by the door (400.12(3)).
Extension cord or cord set left as the permanent supply to a fixed appliance (400.12(1)).
Cord concealed above a suspended ceiling, or attached to building surfaces outside the permitted exceptions (400.12(4), (5)).

sections.title: Uses permitted and not permitted — flexible cords (400.10 / 400.12)
sections.plain_explanation: Sections 400.10 (uses permitted) and 400.12 (uses not permitted) draw the line for flexible cords; 400.7 and 400.8 are the 2017 numbers. Permitted uses are the ones that need to move or be serviced: pendants, portable lamps and appliances, elevator and hoist cables, parts of listed equipment, and similar flexible connections. The not-permitted list is the one that fails inspections: a cord may not substitute for the fixed wiring of a building, run through holes in walls, ceilings, or floors, pass through doorways or windows, attach to building surfaces outside the narrow exceptions, hide inside walls or conduit, or sit where it will be damaged. If a cord is doing a cable's job permanently, it is the wrong wiring method. 400.12, in Code order — flexible cords may not be: (1) a substitute for fixed wiring; (2) run through holes in walls, structural ceilings, suspended or dropped ceilings, or floors; (3) run through doorways, windows or similar openings; (4) attached to building surfaces (except as 368.56(B) and 590.4 permit); (5) concealed by walls, floors or ceilings, or located above suspended or dropped ceilings; (6) installed in raceways except as otherwise permitted; (7) installed where subject to physical damage.
sections.on_the_job: The classic callout: an appliance or tool left cord-connected through a wall or across a doorway 'temporarily' for months. If the load is permanent, price and install a real branch circuit — do not dress up a cord run.
sections.figure_idea: Two-column card: 'cord is fine here' scenes (pendant, portable tool) versus 'hardwire it' scenes (through a wall, under a door).

sections.title: What flexible cords may be used for
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 400.10 lists the jobs a flexible cord is allowed to do: hanging fixtures, connecting portable equipment, appliances that need to be moved for cleaning or service, and similar uses where flexibility is the point. The common thread is that the equipment, not the building, is what moves. A cord feeding a fixed outlet box or a permanent load is outside this list.

Cord ampacity comes from Table 400.5(A)(1) for the cord type and the number of current-carrying conductors — the sizes a crew actually holds, figured for two current-carrying conductors:
• 18 AWG cord — 10 A
• 16 AWG cord — 13 A
• 14 AWG cord — 18 A
• 12 AWG cord — 25 A
• 10 AWG cord — 30 A
A third current-carrying conductor in the same cord drops the value (the table's next column), which is why a cord's rating is read off its own table and not off the building-wire ampacity table.
sections.on_the_job: Before you plug or hard-wire a cord to anything, name the 400.10 use out loud. If you cannot name one, stop and run conduit or cable. Watch especially for cords run through walls, ceilings, or doorways, which this article does not allow.

sections.title: Uses not permitted — flexible cords and cables
sections.plain_explanation: Section 400.12 is the stop list for flexible cords and cables — in the 2017 edition this list was numbered 400.8, and the 2020 reorganization of Article 400 moved it here. Unless 400.10 permits the use, a flexible cord, flexible cable, cord set, or power-supply cord may not be used: (1) as a substitute for the fixed wiring of the structure; (2) run through holes in walls, structural ceilings, suspended or dropped ceilings, or floors; (3) run through doorways, windows, or similar openings; (4) attached to building surfaces, except that cords used for temporary wiring under 590.4 may be attached; (5) concealed by walls, floors, or ceilings, or located above suspended or dropped ceilings, except within an enclosure for use in other spaces used for environmental air as permitted by 300.22(C)(3); (6) installed in raceways, except as 400.17 permits in industrial establishments where only qualified persons service the installation; or (7) where it is subject to physical damage. Most failed 'cord' installations fail here, not on ampacity.
sections.on_the_job: On a service call, trace the whole cord, not just the ends. If any part of it is stapled, hidden, or passing through a partition, the fix is a permanent wiring method, not a heavier cord.

sections.title: Fixture wires — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 402 covers the small conductors used inside fixtures and equipment, called fixture wires. They are for wiring within a luminaire or similar equipment and for connecting that equipment over a limited distance, not for general branch-circuit runs through a building. Sizes run smaller than branch wiring, which is exactly why they must stay inside the equipment they belong to.
• Uses permitted (402.10): inside luminaires and similar equipment, enclosed or protected and not subject to bending or twisting in use, and for connecting luminaires to the branch-circuit conductors that supply them.
• Uses not permitted (402.12): fixture wires are not branch-circuit conductors, except where another article permits them, such as Class 1 remote-control and signaling circuits.
• The smallest size is 18 AWG (402.6), and ampacity comes from Table 402.5, not Table 310.16: 18 AWG is 6 A and 16 AWG is 8 A, whatever the insulation type.
• Protection is by the tap rules (240.5(B)(2)): on a 20 A circuit, an 18 AWG tap may run 50 ft and a 16 AWG tap 100 ft.
sections.on_the_job: If you find a fixture wire run acting like a branch circuit through a wall or ceiling, flag it. Replace that run with a Chapter 3 method sized for the circuit. Keep fixture-wire splices inside the fixture or its listed outlet box. On a high-bay retrofit the pattern is: 12 AWG branch wiring to the box on the 20 A circuit, then the fixture's own 18 AWG whip down to the luminaire. A 25 ft tap is inside the 50 ft limit, and the LED driver draws about 1.5 A against the whip's 6 A ampacity. The wire between two fixtures is not a tap: it is branch wiring, and it stays Chapter 3 wire.
sections.why_it_exists: Fixture wire ratings are figured for the inside of a fixture: short runs, known loads, and the fixture's own heat. Run it through a building like branch wire and a 6 A conductor can end up sitting on a 20 A breaker with nothing to save it. The tap limits in 240.5 are the compromise: short, load-limited whips are fine; a building run is not.
inspection_fails: Fixture wire run through a wall or ceiling as a branch circuit.
18 AWG fixture wire tap over 50 ft long on a 20 A circuit.
Fixture wire spliced in the open, outside the fixture or its listed box.
Fixture wire loaded past its Table 402.5 ampacity.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is reaching for Table 310.16, or for the small-conductor rules, to rate fixture wire. Fixture wire has its own table: 18 AWG is 6 A, not 15 A. The 20 A breaker is allowed behind it only because 240.5(B)(2) treats the whip as a tap with a length limit, not because the wire carries 20 A.

sections.title: Fixture wire ampacity — small wire, small numbers (Table 402.5)
sections.plain_explanation:
Fixture wires are the small conductors inside luminaires and equipment, and Table 402.5 gives them their own ampacities — not the branch-circuit numbers for the same gauge. The whole table is five rows:
• 18 AWG fixture wire — 6 A
• 16 AWG fixture wire — 8 A
• 14 AWG fixture wire — 17 A
• 12 AWG fixture wire — 23 A
• 10 AWG fixture wire — 28 A
Fixture wire is protected and tapped under the fixture-wire rules (240.5), never treated as branch-circuit wire, and it never leaves the fixture or equipment it belongs to. No fixture wire is smaller than 18 AWG (402.6).
sections.on_the_job: Rewiring a fixture whip or a driver lead: match the fixture wire to what the fixture came with. Never extend a circuit with fixture wire because it was handy on the truck. A 16 AWG whip is an 8 A conductor — plenty for an LED driver lead, nowhere near a circuit. Where fixture wire taps a 20 A branch circuit, 240.5(B)(2) caps the run: 18 AWG up to 50 ft, 16 AWG up to 100 ft, and 14 AWG or larger without the length cap.

sections.why_it_exists: Fixture wire runs inside a hot, closed metal box, bundled against ballasts and drivers, in sizes too small to survive a hard fault on a big breaker. Its own ampacity table, and the tap limits in 240.5, keep a fault inside the fixture from turning the whip into a heating element. Extend a run with it, or load it to branch-circuit numbers, and the weak link is hidden where nobody will see it smoke.

sections.title: Switches — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 404 covers switches: the devices that open and close a circuit, from a simple single-pole snap switch to motor-circuit switches. It handles which conductor a switch may interrupt, where a grounded (neutral) conductor must be available at a switch box, how high and how accessible a switch must be, and how switch terminals are marked for conductor materials. The working rules:
• Switching belongs in the ungrounded (hot) conductor — a switch never interrupts the neutral alone (404.2(A)).
• A grounded conductor (neutral) must be present at most switch locations, so electronic controls, timers and sensors can power themselves (404.2(C)). Listed exceptions exist — raceways where the neutral can be pulled in later, certain replacements — so read the exception list for the exact job.
• Switches must be readily accessible, and the center of the operating handle, in its highest position, may not be more than 6 ft 7 in. above the floor or platform (404.8(A)). That is a ceiling, not a mounting height.
Start here whenever a switching question is about the device itself rather than the circuit feeding it.
sections.on_the_job: On rough-in, the two 404 questions to settle before the walls close are neutral availability at switch boxes and switch height. Both are cheap at rough-in and expensive after drywall. Sharma sets switches at 48 in. to the center of the box when the plan is silent (S-05) — a company preference, not a code number; the code only caps the operating handle at 6 ft 7 in. (404.8(A)). Pull the neutral through every switch box on the rough, even where today's device is a plain snap switch: the dimmer or occupancy sensor that replaces it later will need it.
sections.sharma_note: S-05: when the plan is silent, Sharma sets switches at 48 in. to the center of the box. That is a company preference, not an Article 404 requirement.

sections.why_it_exists: A switch is the one part of the circuit a person touches every day, often in the dark, sometimes with wet hands. Switching the hot conductor means the load is dead when the switch is off; switching the neutral leaves the fixture live and waiting. The neutral in the box exists because a generation of dimmers, timers and sensors was stranded in boxes with no way to power itself, and the height ceiling keeps a switch or disconnect within reach of a person standing on the floor.

sections.title: Three-way and four-way switching — what the switch may control
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 404.2(A) is about which conductor a switch interrupts. For three-way and four-way switches the rule is stated outright: all switching must be in the ungrounded (hot) conductor.
• The grounded (neutral) conductor is never switched. It runs unbroken to the load and lands on the screw shell of a lampholder, so the shell — the part fingers touch — stays on the grounded side.
• In a traveler system, the hot lands on the first switch's common terminal, the two travelers carry it from switch to switch, and the switched leg leaves the last switch's common for the load. Two or more locations control one load while the rule stays intact.
• The banned pattern is the old Carter system: hot and neutral both landed on the traveler terminals, so depending on the switch positions the shell could sit on the hot side — with the light off. Prohibited since the 1923 NEC, it still turns up in old Florida houses.
sections.on_the_job: Wire 3-way/4-way runs by function, not by color habit: common, travelers, switched leg, neutral, ground. On a Sharma house rough-in — a Winter Park two-story with switches at both ends of the hall and at the top and bottom of the stairs — the travelers on the long runs get labeled at rough-in, per the Sharma practice note below, so the trim crew is not ringing out pairs through finished walls. Test every switch position at trim and confirm the load is fully controlled from each location before you leave. Never borrow a neutral from another circuit to make a traveler scheme work.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma practice note (job practice, not code text): label travelers at rough-in when a run is long or passes through several boxes. It saves the trim crew from ringing out pairs.
sections.figure_idea: Figure idea (original, ours): a simple line drawing in our own style showing one load, a 3-way at each end and a 4-way in the middle, with boxes labelled common / travelers / switched leg — no textbook diagram copied.
sections.why_it_exists: A lamp that is 'off' should be safe to re-lamp. If the switching scheme leaves the screw shell connected to a hot conductor, the person changing the bulb — standing on a ladder, one hand on the shell — becomes the path. Switching only the hot conductor, and keeping the shell on the grounded conductor, is what makes 'off' mean off.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is wiring by 'it works.' A Carter-wired 3-way turns the light on and off from both locations, so it passes a lazy test — but in some switch combinations the socket shell is hot with the light off. 'The light works from both switches' is not the test; 'all switching is in the ungrounded conductor' is. The same goes for landing a traveler on the common because the colors looked right.
inspection_fails: Neutral switched instead of the hot — the lampholder shell stays energized with the light off (404.2(A)).
Carter-style wiring found or recreated: hot and neutral both on the traveler terminals.
Traveler landed on a common terminal, so the load obeys only one switch or the positions disagree.
Neutral borrowed from another circuit to make a traveler scheme work.

sections.title: A neutral must be available at most switch locations
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 404.2(C) requires a grounded conductor — the neutral — to be installed at the switch locations where switches control lighting loads on a grounded general-purpose branch circuit: bathrooms, hallways, stairways, and habitable rooms. The reason is practical: modern controls, timers, occupancy sensors and smart switches need a neutral to power themselves.
• The neutral must be there even if today's device is a plain snap switch that never touches it.
• Where 3-way or 4-way locations control the same load and the whole floor area is visible from the switch locations, the neutral is required at only one location.
• Exceptions (2020) let you omit it where the conductors enter through a raceway with room to add the neutral later, where a cable can still be added or replaced without removing finish materials, for snap switches with integral enclosures complying with 300.15(E), where the lighting is controlled by automatic means, and where the switch controls a receptacle load.
Read the exception list for the exact job instead of assuming — and pull the neutral anyway when in doubt.
sections.on_the_job: At rough-in, pull the neutral through every switch box even when the planned device is a plain snap switch that does not use it today. Cap it neatly in the back of the box. That one habit prevents the most common 404.2(C) correction and makes later smart-switch work possible without opening walls. On a Marion Oaks entry, the 3-gang box gets the feed, three switch legs, and the neutral spliced through and capped; the hall 3-ways need the neutral at one location only, because the whole hall is visible from both ends.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma note: this is why the Honeywell / ecobee-era control work and smart switches on Sharma jobs assume a neutral in the box. Do not design a switch location that strands a future electronic control without one.

nec2023_change.change: One escape hatch for skipping the neutral at lighting switches is gone: a box you can get into later without opening up the finish no longer counts. Gone in 2023: the pass for a switch box reachable later without removing finish materials. Pull the neutral anyway (404.2(C)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 404.2 Neutral at switch locations

sections.why_it_exists: Electronic controls need power while the light is off. Without a neutral in the box, the old workarounds leaked current through the load or borrowed the equipment ground — flickering lamps and current on grounding paths. Requiring the neutral at rough-in, while the walls are open, turns every later control swap into a device change instead of a demolition job.

Neutral present in the box, but from a different circuit than the switch leg it serves.

sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'no neutral needed — the specified device is a plain snap switch.' The rule is about the location, not today's device: if the switch controls lighting in a habitable room, the neutral goes in the box. The related trap is powering a smart switch by borrowing the equipment grounding conductor as its return — electronic control switches are not permitted to put their operating current on the ground (404.22).

sections.title: Switches in damp or wet locations — and out of the tub/shower wet location
sections.plain_explanation: Article 404 requires switches installed in damp or wet locations to be in enclosures suited to the location, and it separately restricts switches in a bathtub or shower space: a switch may not be installed within the wet location of a tub or shower unless it is part of a listed tub or shower assembly made for that purpose. The rule parallels the receptacle and luminaire zones in 406.9(C) and 410.10(D) — the wettest part of the room is kept free of devices a wet person would operate. A switch on the dry wall outside that space is an ordinary installation.
sections.on_the_job: At layout, treat the tub/shower wet location as a no-switch zone the same way you treat it as a no-receptacle zone. Exterior and patio switches get weatherproof enclosures suited to whether a cover must close over a plug or cord. Pool and spa switching also answers to Article 680 — check Chapter 6 before you place a switch near water.
sections.florida_note: Florida note: outdoor kitchens, lanais, and pool-adjacent switching are damp or wet locations in practice; enclosure choice matters more here than the switch itself.

sections.title: Switches must be reachable — operating handle height
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 404.8(A) requires switches to be readily accessible and sets a ceiling on height: the center of the operating handle, in its highest position, may not be more than 6 ft 7 in. above the floor or working platform. The point is that a person standing on the floor must be able to operate the switch without a ladder or a reach tool. It does not set the normal mounting height for a house switch — that comes from the plan or company practice.
• The measurement is to the center of the handle with the handle up — not to the top of the box or the plate.
• Special cases exist for switches next to the equipment they serve and for busway-type installations, so check the exceptions before you relocate a switch that looks too high.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma roughs house switches at 48 in. to the center of the box when the plan is silent (S-05), so the ceiling in 404.8(A) rarely comes up — until it does. On an Ocala final, the garage switch for the yard lights had been set high to clear a workbench: the center of the handle in the up position measured 6 ft 8 in. One inch over the limit, and it failed. It moved down to 5 ft 6 in., still clear of the bench.
sections.sharma_note: S-05: Sharma's default is 48 in. to the center of the box when the plan is silent. The plan governs when it states a height. Do not present 48 in. as a code number — 404.8(A) is the code ceiling, S-05 is our working height.
sections.why_it_exists: A switch is the control a person reaches for in the dark, in smoke, or in a hurry. If it takes a ladder or a broom handle, it is not really a control — people leave the light on, or worse, cannot shut a circuit off at the device. The 6 ft 7 in. ceiling keeps every switch within a standing person's reach.

The code gives a maximum, not a mounting height: 6 ft 7 in. to the center of the operating handle in its highest position. The second trap is measuring to the top of the box — the rule measures the handle.

sections.title: Grounding snap switches (404.9)
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 404.9 requires snap switches — including dimmers and control switches — to be connected to an equipment grounding conductor (EGC), so the metal yoke and any metal faceplate are bonded.
• Metal box: the box is bonded by its EGC, and the switch's mounting screws bond the yoke to the box (250.109). The screws are the bond — use the switch's own mounting screws, tight.
• Nonmetallic box: there is no box to bond through, so the EGC lands on the switch's own green grounding terminal.
• Faceplates: 404.9(A) also requires the plate to completely cover the box opening and seat against the finished surface.
The replacement exception matters in old houses. Where an existing switch is replaced in a box with no grounding means — no EGC in the wiring method — an ungrounded replacement is permitted for replacement only, on the exception's terms: a nonmetallic, noncombustible faceplate with nonmetallic screws, or GFCI protection for the circuit. Where the switch sits within 8 ft vertically or 5 ft horizontally of ground or exposed grounded metal objects, those terms are the whole allowance. Landing a standard switch with a metal plate on a 2-wire box and moving on is not one of the paths.
sections.on_the_job: On remodels, check for a ground before trim-out, not during the final walk. In a 1960s Orlando ranch wired with 2-wire cable, Sharma's crew found no EGC in any switch box on the lighting circuits. Because the panel was being replaced with new Siemens gear anyway, the fix was GFCI breakers on those lighting circuits, which puts every replacement switch on the exception's GFCI path; on the one circuit that stayed unprotected, the plates went on nonmetallic, with nonmetallic screws. No EGC in the box changes what devices you may land — flag it at discovery.
sections.figure_idea: Yoke-to-box bond sketch: EGC to a metal box with the switch screws bonding the yoke; green terminal to EGC in a plastic box.
sections.why_it_exists: The yoke and the plate screws sit right where fingers land in the dark. If a hot conductor faults to an unbonded yoke, the plate and its screws sit at line voltage with nothing to trip the breaker, and the first person to touch the switch becomes the fault path. The EGC gives that fault a low-impedance road home, so the breaker opens instead.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'The switch is in a metal box, so it is grounded.' A metal box is a grounding path only when the box itself is connected to an EGC. A steel box fed by old 2-wire cable bonds the yoke to a floating box — worse than plastic if the box ever faults. The second trap: GFCI protection does not create a ground. It is the exception's alternative protection for a replacement, not an equipment ground.

sections.title: Snap switch ratings and the loads they may control
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 404.14 ties a general-use snap switch to the kind of load it controls. A switch marked for AC only, or for AC/DC, has different limits for motor, inductive, and tungsten-type loads, and a switch may not be loaded past the rating that applies to that load type. In plain terms: the amp number on the yoke is not a promise for every load — the load type decides which limit applies.

The working limits, by load type:
• Resistive loads — up to the switch's full marked ampere rating
• Inductive loads (ballasts, transformers) — full rating on an AC general-use switch; 50 percent of the rating on an AC/DC general-use switch
• Motor loads — 80 percent of the rating on an AC general-use switch, or the switch's marked horsepower rating where it has one
• Tungsten-filament lamp loads — full rating at 120V on an AC general-use snap switch (404.14(A)); the 'T' rating question applies to AC/DC switches (404.14(B))
Worked example: a 15A AC-only snap switch may carry a 12A motor load (15 × 0.80) and up to 15A of tungsten lighting at 120V; the 'T' marking question applies to AC/DC switches.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 404.14: Switch terminals now have wire rules: copper or copper-clad aluminum unless CO/ALR, and push-in holes are for 14 AWG solid copper, only on 15-amp circuits. Dimmers now follow the same load rule as timers. Push-in (back-stab) holes take only 14 AWG solid copper on a 15-amp circuit, unless the switch is listed and marked for other wire (404.14(D)).

sections.on_the_job: Read the yoke marking before you put a snap switch on a motor, a ballast bank, or a heater. Where the load is a motor or is otherwise hard on contacts, use a switch rated for that duty or control it through a rated contactor or relay.

sections.title: Switch terminal markings for conductor materials (CO/ALR)
sections.plain_explanation: Section 404.15(C) carries the CO/ALR marking rule for switches — the switch-side twin of 406.3(C) for receptacles: a switch designed for the direct connection of aluminum conductors must be marked CO/ALR. The terminal rules that go with the marking, stated for the 2020 NEC in NEMA Engineering Bulletin No. 122 from the UL guide information for snap switches: terminals of 15A and 20A snap switches are for use with copper and copper-clad aluminum conductors only, unless marked CO/ALR, which adds aluminum; terminals of switches rated 30A and above are for copper only, unless marked AL/CU. Plain aluminum never lands on an unmarked device terminal.
sections.on_the_job: Check the device itself: read the terminal marking on the switch you are holding and match it to the conductor you are landing — no CO/ALR marking, no plain aluminum on the terminal. Do not backstab CCA — Sharma lands CCA on screw terminals only (see S-10).
sections.sharma_note: S-10 applies: CCA is sized one AWG larger than copper and terminations must be listed for the conductor. Never backstab.

sections.title: Receptacles, cord connectors, and attachment plugs — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 406 covers receptacle outlets and the plugs and cord connectors that go into them: how receptacles are rated and grounded, when a replacement must upgrade protection, where face-up devices may be used, what damp and wet locations demand, the tub and shower exclusion zone, and where tamper-resistant receptacles are required. It is the article behind most device-level corrections on a residential final.
• Ratings, grounding and replacements (406.4): receptacles match the circuit's rating and configuration, are grounding type where the wiring method provides a ground, and a replacement follows the 406.4(D) upgrade ladder, including GFCI protection and 'No Equipment Ground' marking where no grounding means exists.
• Damp and wet locations (406.9): weather-resistant receptacles and the covers the location demands.
• Tub and shower zone (406.9(C)): no receptacles within a zone measured 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of the tub rim or shower stall threshold.
• Tamper-resistant (406.12): TR receptacles in dwelling units and the other listed occupancies, with exceptions such as receptacles more than 5-1/2 ft above the floor.
sections.on_the_job: At trim, work 406 as a checklist room by room: correct replacement type, WR where the location needs it, in-use cover where the location is wet, TR where 406.12 requires it, and nothing inside the tub/shower zone. The bathroom is where the zone bites: the basin receptacle has to sit within 3 ft of the basin (210.52(D)) and still stay out of the 3 ft by 8 ft zone measured from the tub rim, so measure from the rim, not from the basin, before the box is set.
sections.sharma_note: S-07: points marked GFI on a Sharma plan get a standard tamper-resistant receptacle protected by the dual-function breaker. Sharma does not install GFCI receptacles as the standard device.

nec2023_change.change: One section, 406.2, now holds the no-reconditioning rule for receptacles, cord connectors, plugs and flanged surface devices. The ban itself dates to 2020. None of these four can be reconditioned: receptacles, attachment plugs (caps), cord connectors and flanged surface inlets or outlets.

sections.title: Receptacle installation and replacement — the general rules (406.4(A)–(C))
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 406.4 sets the baseline before the replacement details in 406.4(D). Receptacles must be of the grounding type where the wiring method provides a ground, must match the circuit's rating and configuration, and replacements follow a ladder: grounding-type for grounding-type where an EGC exists; where no grounding means exists, the permitted paths are a nongrounding replacement, a GFCI replacement marked 'No Equipment Ground,' or a grounding-type receptacle fed through a GFCI and marked the same way. The markings are part of the rule, not paperwork. where an EGC exists or is connected under 250.130(C), the replacement is a grounding-type receptacle (406.4(D)(1)). Third replacement option, exactly: a grounding-type receptacle supplied through a GFCI, marked 'GFCI Protected' and 'No Equipment Ground' (406.4(D)(2)(c)).

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 406.4: Food court and transit waiting-area floor receptacles now need GFCI, a CO/ALR replacement on aluminum wire can skip tamper-resistant, and a replacement must provide GFPE wherever GFPE is now required. GFCI now covers 125-volt, 15- and 20-amp floor receptacles in food courts and airport, bus and train waiting areas that allow food or drink (406.4(G)(2)).

sections.title: Replacing a receptacle — the replacement must meet today's rules for that location
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 406.4(D) governs what you must do when you swap out an existing receptacle. Where current code requires GFCI, AFCI, tamper-resistant, or weather-resistant protection at that location, the replacement has to provide it. Where there is no equipment grounding conductor in the box, the permitted paths are a non-grounding-type replacement, a GFCI-type replacement marked as having no equipment ground, or a grounding-type receptacle fed through a GFCI device and marked accordingly. You may not simply install a standard grounding receptacle on an ungrounded circuit and leave it looking grounded.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 406.4(D)(3): Substantiation was provided to that will require ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) receptacles to be listed per 406.4(D)(3).
• 406.4(D)(8): Substantiation has been provided to to require ground-fault protection of equipment (GFPE) to be provided for replacement receptacles that require GFPE protection by current Code requirements elsewhere in the NEC
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: On a service swap, test for a real ground first, then pick the replacement path and apply the required marking sticker or engraving before you leave. Photograph the marking for the job record when it is a no-equipment-ground installation.
sections.sharma_note: S-07 note: on new Sharma work the GFCI/AFCI protection lives at the DFN breaker, so a replacement on a Sharma DFN circuit normally keeps a standard TR device. On older panels without that protection, 406.4(D) is what forces the upgrade at the device.

sections.title: Receptacle assemblies in countertops and work surfaces — listed for the surface
sections.plain_explanation:
A receptacle assembly installed in a countertop surface has to be listed for countertop applications — an ordinary receptacle in a cut-in box does not become countertop equipment by being set into the surface.
• Where the assembly is required to provide GFCI protection under 210.8, it is permitted to be a GFCI receptacle assembly listed for countertop applications.
• Section 406.5(F) applies the same listing rule to receptacle assemblies in work surfaces.
• Whether a receptacle may sit face-up in that surface at all is the next rule, 406.5(G): face-up is allowed only for assemblies listed for countertop or work surface use, and never in the area below a sink.
The listing is the point: a countertop assembly is tested for the spills, heat and cleaning that a countertop actually sees.
sections.on_the_job: On a Winter Park kitchen island, the plan shows one receptacle in the island top and one on the cabinet side. The one in the top goes on the material list as a listed pop-up countertop assembly — the GFCI version, because kitchen countertop receptacles need GFCI protection under 210.8. The side receptacle is an ordinary tamper-resistant duplex in the cabinet side; it is not in the surface, so 406.5(E) does not govern it. Do not let the counter fabricator cut a hole sized for a standard duplex in the stone.
sections.figure_idea: Section through a kitchen island: a listed pop-up countertop assembly with its listing tag called out, beside a standard duplex in a cut box with a red X.
sections.why_it_exists: A countertop is a wet work surface. Liquids spill, pots overflow, and crumbs and metal utensils sit on it all day. An ordinary receptacle face set into that surface collects whatever lands on it, straight into the slots. A listed countertop assembly is built and tested for that exposure — sealed, spill-shedding, and made to be cleaned.
inspection_fails: Standard duplex receptacle cut into a quartz island top.
Desk or grommet outlet assembly used in a kitchen counter — not listed for countertop applications.
Countertop assembly without GFCI protection where 210.8 requires it.
Face-up receptacle installed in the counter area below the sink.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'any receptacle can go in the countertop as long as it is GFCI protected.' GFCI protection and countertop listing are different requirements — the assembly must be listed for countertop applications. The reverse trap is 'face-up receptacles are banned everywhere': a listed countertop assembly may sit face-up, just never in the area below a sink.

sections.title: Face-up receptacles in countertops — the prohibition is 406.5(G)
sections.plain_explanation: Section 406.5(G) carries the face-up rule for receptacles in counters and work surfaces. Under (G)(1), a receptacle may not be installed in a face-up position in or on a countertop or work surface unless it is listed for countertop or work surface applications. Under (G)(2), a receptacle may not be installed face-up in the area below a sink at all — the listed-assembly exception does not apply there. The hazard is the position itself: a face-up device collects spills, crumbs, and liquids directly into its face. The separate listing rule for receptacle assemblies made for these surfaces is at 406.5(E) and (F), covered on the previous page.
sections.on_the_job: Do not cut a standard duplex into a countertop face-up. Put the receptacle on the side of the cabinet or on the wall at the backsplash, or use a listed pop-up assembly made for countertop use — a listed assembly is the one face-up exception 406.5(G)(1) allows. Nothing goes face-up in the area below a sink.

sections.title: Receptacles in damp locations
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 406.9(A) covers receptacles in damp locations — places that are protected from direct weather but can be damp, such as a covered porch or a carport. Damp is the middle category: not dry indoors, not taking direct rain.
• The receptacle must be weather-resistant (WR) type. On houses and light commercial work that means the 15 A and 20 A, 125 V and 250 V devices — the same WR devices 406.9(B) requires in wet locations.
• The enclosure must keep moisture out of the wiring connections when no plug is inserted. A cover that is weatherproof when the plug is out — the flip lid — is the usual way this is met.
• The cover does not have to stay weatherproof while a cord is plugged in. The in-use (bubble) cover belongs to the wet-location rule, 406.9(B).
sections.on_the_job: Covered lanai on a Florida home: the receptacles sit under the roof, but afternoon storms blow mist across them — that is damp, not dry. Fit WR receptacles and flip-lid covers that close weatherproof with nothing plugged in. Look up before you decide: if the device can get rained on with the cover open or closed — past the roof drip line, or under a leaking gutter — treat it as wet, not damp, and use the 406.9(B) arrangement: a WR receptacle plus a listed extra-duty in-use cover. When in doubt, install the wet-location setup — it satisfies the damp case too.
sections.why_it_exists: Damp air, condensation and wind-blown mist corrode contacts and creep across damp surfaces inside a box. A receptacle that is not weather-resistant loses contact pressure and insulation resistance after a few Florida summers, and an enclosure that lets moisture sit on the connections does the same damage from outside. The rule keeps the damp away from the device and its wiring connections.
inspection_fails: Standard (non-WR) receptacle installed on a covered porch or in a carport.
No cover, or a cover that is not weatherproof with the plug removed, so moisture sits in the box.
Receptacle past the roof drip line treated as damp — it takes direct rain and needs the wet-location in-use cover.
Indoor cover plate on a damp-location box, or the gasket missing and the cover hanging open.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is calling a covered porch a dry location. Covered and protected from direct rain is the definition of a damp location, and the receptacle still has to be WR type with a cover that is weatherproof when the plug is out. The other wrong pick is the bubble cover: damp locations do not require an in-use cover — that requirement is 406.9(B), the wet rule.

sections.title: Receptacles in wet locations — in-use covers and weather-resistant devices
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 406.9(B) covers receptacles in wet locations, where water can reach the device whether or not something is plugged in. The enclosure must stay weatherproof while a plug is inserted and the cord is in use — the bubble or in-use cover — and 15A and 20A, 125V and 250V receptacles in wet locations must be weather-resistant (WR) type. An unattended wet-location receptacle, such as one on a house exterior, needs that in-use protection; the rule has specific treatment for receptacles that are attended while in use.

Two details decide inspections here. First, the in-use cover (the outlet box hood) for a wet-location receptacle must be listed and identified as extra duty — the heavier hinged cover — where 406.9(B)(1) requires it; a light flip lid is a damp-location part, not a wet-location one. Second, the weather-resistant requirement in this section reaches the 15A and 20A, 125V and 250V receptacles a house and a light commercial job actually use; larger pin-and-sleeve and locking devices follow their own listing for the location.
sections.on_the_job: Stock both parts on the truck: a WR receptacle and an extra-duty in-use cover. A flat flip lid on an exterior receptacle that runs a pump, a charger, or landscape equipment is a correction waiting to happen. Seat the cover gasket fully and route the cord out the bottom notch so the cover can close.
sections.florida_note: Florida note: afternoon rain and irrigation spray make most Florida exterior receptacles wet locations in practice, whatever the plan calls them. Default to WR + in-use cover outside.

sections.title: No receptacles inside the tub or shower zone
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 406.9(C) keeps receptacles out of the zone directly inside and immediately around a bathtub or shower stall. In the 2020 arrangement this zone is measured 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of the bathtub rim or the shower stall threshold, and no receptacle may be installed within that zone. The rule exists because a person in water is in the worst possible position to contact a device or a cord connected to it.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 406.9(C): Clarified receptacle restrictions in and around bathtubs and showers in Section 406.9(C). A new Exception #4 was added to allow single receptacles within 36" of the tub or shower with limitations.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: On layout, mark the zone on the floor plan before you place bath receptacles, not at trim. Vanity receptacles belong outside the zone even when the counter runs close to the tub. If the only wall space is inside the zone, move the discussion to the builder before rough-in, not to the inspector at final.

sections.title: Tamper-resistant receptacles in dwellings and other listed occupancies
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 406.12 requires tamper-resistant receptacles in dwelling units and in a list of other occupancies where children are present, such as guest rooms, childcare and preschool areas, dormitories, and certain medical and office waiting areas. A TR receptacle has internal shutters that only open when both blades of a plug go in together, so a key or paperclip pushed into one slot does not reach a live contact. The requirement applies at the receptacle locations the article covers, generally those at normal reachable height rather than the listed exceptions such as receptacles high above the floor or inside a luminaire.

The exceptions matter on service work. The TR requirement does not reach:
• Receptacles located more than 5-1/2 ft above the floor
• Receptacles that are part of a luminaire or an appliance
• A single receptacle for one appliance, or a duplex for two, in the dedicated space for an appliance that is not easily moved in normal use
• Nongrounding-type replacements installed under 406.4(D) where the box has no grounding means
Everything else at normal device height in the occupancies this section lists is TR — when in doubt, the TR device is the answer.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 406.12: The tamper-resistant (TR) list grew to ten location groups, adding boathouses, fitness centers, group homes, rehab facilities, nursing homes, foster care, psychiatric hospitals and farm buildings open to the public. Item (1) now lists boathouses, mobile homes and manufactured homes by name, along with dwelling units and their garages, outbuildings and common areas.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Use TR devices as the default dwelling device and check the exception before you substitute a standard one. A failed shutter on a damaged TR receptacle means replacement, not a standard-device swap (see 406.4(D)).

sections.title: Switchboards, switchgear, and panelboards — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 408 covers the boards themselves: switchboards, switchgear, and the panelboards Sharma installs on nearly every job. For residential and light commercial work, the live parts of this article are:
• The circuit directory: every circuit identified specifically at the board, spares marked as spares (408.4(A)).
• Identification of the source of supply where a board is fed from another board (408.4(B)).
• A short-circuit current rating at least equal to the available fault current (408.6).
• Unused openings closed with closures listed for the enclosure (408.7).
• Overcurrent protection of the panelboard itself, at no more than the panelboard's rating (408.36).
• One grounded (neutral) conductor per terminal (408.41).
• Breakers of the type listed for the panel they sit in.
The industrial switchboard sections matter on larger commercial gear; the directory and listing rules matter everywhere.
sections.on_the_job: Treat the panel as a document, not just a box: directory filled in, circuits identified at every disconnect, unused openings closed, and only listed breakers installed. An inspector can fail a beautiful rough-in on a blank directory. On a Sharma trim, that means a new Siemens board (S-02) with the directory written from the actual schedule and checked circuit by circuit, spares marked 'SPARE,' and every open space closed with the Siemens filler listed for that panel. In an existing Square D panel, only Square D breakers listed for that panel go in (S-03). And check the protection: a 100 A panelboard never sits behind a 200 A breaker just because the feeder is big (408.36).
sections.sharma_note: S-02: all new Sharma gear is Siemens. S-03: in an existing Square D panel, install Square D breakers listed for that panel — never mix brands to fill a space.

nec2023_change.change: The enclosure rule now ties to fault current: once available fault current passes 10,000 amps, the panelboard and its enclosure have to be evaluated as a matched combination. If available fault current tops 10,000 amps, the interior and its enclosure need to be evaluated as one combination.

sections.why_it_exists: The panelboard is where every circuit in the building starts, and where fault energy is highest. A board protected above its bus rating, fitted with breakers it was never listed for, or left with open spaces becomes the failure point itself. The directory rules exist because the next person — a servicer, a firefighter, a homeowner at midnight — has to kill the right circuit fast, and a wrong label sends them to the wrong breaker.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: 'Any breaker that snaps into the panel is fine.' It is not. A breaker must be listed for that panelboard — a foreign breaker that physically fits still voids the listing and draws a correction. The companion trap: protecting a 100 A panelboard with a 200 A breaker because the feeder conductors are large. Section 408.36 protects the bus, not the wire.
inspection_fails: Circuit directory blank, generic ('lights,' 'plugs'), or not updated after a circuit change (408.4(A)).
Unused breaker opening left open, or closed with tape instead of a listed filler plate (408.7).
Breaker of another brand installed in the panel — not listed for that panelboard.
100 A panelboard protected by a 200 A overcurrent device (408.36).
Panelboard SCCR below the available fault current at a commercial service (408.6).

sections.title: The circuit directory — specific, on site, and kept current
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 408.4(A) requires every circuit and circuit modification to be identified at the panelboard with enough detail to tell circuits apart, and a circuit directory (or circuit identification) must be provided at the board. Generic labels like 'plugs,' 'lights,' or 'bedroom' written for a different house do not meet the intent; the identification has to describe the actual purpose or use of each circuit in that building. Spare positions must be marked as spares, and the directory must be updated when circuits change.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 408.4(A): Circuit directory rules became a six-part checklist that now requires explaining any abbreviations or symbols. In buildings other than one- and two-family homes, feeder-fed panels must also show where their source physically sits. Feeder-supplied panels outside one- and two-family dwellings must name the equipment feeding them and where it physically is (408.4(B)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Fill the directory at trim, from the actual panel schedule, and have the person who wired the house check it circuit by circuit with a tester or by switching. A directory copied from the plan without field verification is how 'Kitchen' ends up feeding the water heater.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma note: the directory is part of the finished product the builder sees. Neat, specific, and correct — 'NE bedroom receptacles,' not 'BR.'

sections.title: Identification of the source of supply
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 408.4(B) addresses panelboards supplied by a feeder: the board must be marked to identify where its supply comes from when that source is in a different location or is not obvious, so that a person standing at the panel can find the disconnect that kills it. Companion identification rules in Article 408 also require disconnects and circuits to be marked for their purpose where they are not self-evident. The theme of the whole part is that nobody should have to guess what feeds what.

• 408.4: Circuit directory rules became a six-part checklist that now requires explaining any abbreviations or symbols. In buildings other than one- and two-family homes, feeder-fed panels must also show where their source physically sits. Feeder-supplied panels outside one- and two-family dwellings must name the equipment feeding them and where it physically is (408.4(B)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

sections.title: The equipment's short-circuit current rating must cover the available fault current
sections.plain_explanation: Section 408.6 requires switchboards, switchgear, and panelboards to have a short-circuit current rating (SCCR) at least equal to the available fault current where they are installed. A panel that matches the job on volts and amps can still be the wrong panel if its SCCR is below the fault current the service can deliver into a short. This requirement was added in the 2020 edition, which is why older change-out habits never asked the question.
sections.on_the_job: On a service change or a commercial panel set, get the available fault current (from the utility or the design documents) and compare it with the SCCR marked on the gear before the gear is ordered. Record both numbers in the job file. If the fault current is unknown, that is an engineering question for Mike, not a field estimate.
sections.sharma_note: S-02 pairs with this page: new Sharma gear is Siemens, and the SCCR check is part of selecting it, not an afterthought at inspection.

sections.title: Unused openings must be closed
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 408.7 requires unused openings in a panelboard, switchboard or switchgear to be closed with closures that give protection substantially equal to the wall of the enclosure.
• A spare breaker space with no breaker in it is an unused opening: it takes the manufacturer's listed filler plate or blank.
• An unused knockout in the enclosure wall is the same problem in a smaller hole: close it with a listed knockout closure.
• Tape is not a closure. Neither are cardboard, foam, or a near-fit plate from another brand.
An open space is an exposed live-part opening, a dust and vermin path, and an automatic correction on inspection.
sections.on_the_job: Keep listed filler plates for the panel brand on the trim truck. Before final, open every panel, run a finger check for open spaces, blank plates, and missing knock-out closures, and close them with the manufacturer's part. On a Sharma job the panel is Siemens, so the fillers on the truck are Siemens fillers: a near-fit plate from another brand is a correction waiting to happen (S-02/S-03).
sections.sharma_note: S-02/S-03 apply to the closure as well: use the filler listed for that panel, not a near-fit from another brand.
sections.why_it_exists: The bus behind the deadfront stays live even where no breaker is installed. An open space lets fingers, a dropped screwdriver or a curious kid reach it, and it lets dust and roaches build up on the bus until tracking and a short do the rest. A closure as strong as the enclosure wall keeps the box a box.
inspection_fails: Spare breaker space left open with no filler plate: live bus exposed behind the deadfront.
Duct tape or cardboard over an unused opening. Neither is a closure.
Unused knockout in the side of the panel never closed.
Filler plate from a different panel brand forced into the space: not the listed closure for that panel.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating an empty breaker space as harmless because nothing is connected to it. The opening itself is the violation: the live bus stab sits right behind it. 'We will add a breaker later' does not close the hole today.

sections.title: The panelboard itself must be protected
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 408.36 requires a panelboard to be protected by an overcurrent device rated no higher than the panelboard's rating, located within the panelboard or at any point ahead of it on the supply side. In plain terms, a 100 A panel may not sit behind a 200 A breaker just because the feeder wires are large. The bus has its own limit and something must enforce it. The exceptions are narrow:
• Exception No. 1: service equipment with multiple disconnecting means under 230.71 (the split-bus case); with three or more mains, they may not supply a second bus structure.
• Exception No. 2: two main breakers or two sets of fuses on the supply side with a combined rating not over the panelboard rating — and no more than 42 overcurrent devices in the board, counting a 2-pole as two and a 3-pole as three.
• Exception No. 3: existing panelboards used as service equipment for an individual residential occupancy.
A panelboard supplied from a transformer under 240.21(C) gets its protection on the secondary side — in a separate enclosure ahead of the board, or in the board itself (408.36(B)).
sections.on_the_job: When you set a sub-panel, check three numbers together: panel bus rating, feeder conductor ampacity, and the breaker feeding it. The smallest applicable limit governs. Record all three on the panel schedule for the office file. Sharma's light-commercial habit: a 100 A Siemens sub-panel gets a 100 A feeder breaker even when the feeder conductors could carry more — the breaker is protecting the bus, not just the wire.

sections.why_it_exists: Feeder conductors are sized for the load and the run; a panelboard bus is built for its rating and nothing more. Put a 100 A bus behind a 200 A breaker and an overload inside the board can push twice the bus rating through stabs and bus bars that were never built for it — the breaker sits happy while the panel cooks. Section 408.36 makes the board's own rating a ceiling that some device, in the board or ahead of it, must enforce.

The reverse trap is calling every split-bus service a violation — the 230.71 multiple-disconnect arrangement is Exception No. 1, not a defect.

sections.title: Each grounded (neutral) conductor gets its own terminal
sections.plain_explanation: Section 408.41 requires each grounded conductor in a panelboard to terminate in its own individual terminal that is not used for any other conductor, unless the terminal is specifically identified for more than one. Doubling two neutrals under one screw is a classic correction: when one circuit is worked on, loosening the shared terminal can open the neutral of a live circuit sharing it. Equipment grounding conductors follow their own termination rules and the panel's listing; the one-per-terminal discipline on this page is about the grounded conductors.
sections.on_the_job: At trim, land neutrals one to a screw and torque them; never park a second neutral under a screw 'temporarily.' On a panel change-out, budget the time to separate doubled neutrals — finding them is part of the job, and the directory update in 408.4(A) happens on the same visit.

sections.title: A panelboard may not be installed face-up
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 408.43 prohibits installing a panelboard in a face-up position. A load center belongs on a vertical surface with its breakers oriented as the listing intends; a face-up board collects debris and water, and its breakers do not operate or indicate as designed. The rule was added in the 2020 edition and most often matters on custom commercial millwork and unusual equipment layouts, not on a standard house panel.
• Legal: the panelboard's front faces a wall — breakers in their listed, vertical orientation.
• Banned since 2020: face-up, front pointing at the ceiling.
• Still legal under the 2020 book, banned in 2023: face-down, front pointing at the floor — see the edition note.
sections.on_the_job: If a plan or a cabinet detail shows a panel lying flat, stop at rough-in and raise it with the builder — the fix is a layout change, not a field workaround. Check orientation on any pre-built equipment package before it is set. On a Sharma commercial job, the millwork detail for a coffee-bar cabinet showed the load center flat under the counter: the cabinet grew a vertical section at rough-in, the panel went on it upright, and the directory (408.4(A)) stayed readable standing in front of it.

nec2023_change.change: Panelboards can't be installed facing down now. Added to the 2020 face-up ban, a panelboard's front can point neither at the ceiling nor at the floor. A panelboard can't be mounted face-down, with its front pointing at the floor, such as on the underside of a ceiling or platform.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 408.43 Panelboards can't face up or down

sections.why_it_exists: A panelboard is a listed assembly tested in one orientation. Lay it face-up and the gutter becomes a tray: dust, screws, water and whatever the next trade drops all land on live parts and breaker mechanisms. Breakers lying flat also do not trip, reset or read the way their listing assumes. The rule keeps the equipment in the only position it was ever evaluated in.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'face-up is fine if the cover stays on' — 408.43 bans the position outright, cover or not. The subtler trap is the calendar: face-down is banned only in the 2023 edition. On a 2020 permit a face-down board is bad practice but not a 408.43 violation; on a 2023 permit it fails.

sections.title: Industrial control panels — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 409 covers industrial control panels: the factory- or field-assembled panels that control industrial machinery and equipment. The article sets the rules for the panel's short-circuit current rating (SCCR) marking, supply conductor sizing, and internal wiring and grounding.
• The SCCR is the headline item. The panel must be marked with it (409.110), and a panel may not be installed where the available fault current at its supply exceeds the rating marked on it.
• Read the label before the panel is set: supply voltage, phases, full-load current, and SCCR all come off the manufacturer's marking.
• Supply conductors are sized from the panel's marked ratings, and the panel's grounding follows 409.60.
Sharma meets this article on light commercial and equipment work rather than in houses — rooftop equipment, lift stations, and machine controls.
sections.on_the_job: Read the SCCR on the panel label and compare it with the available fault current at its supply before you set the panel. On a light-commercial equipment swap in Orlando, the utility letter put the available fault current at 22 kA. The replacement control panel's label read 10 kA SCCR — that panel does not get set, no matter that its breakers are rated 22 kA; the assembly's marked SCCR is the ceiling. A panel marked 65 kA SCCR clears the same supply with room to spare. If the panel has no SCCR marking or the fault current is unknown, stop and take it to Mike — that is an engineering check, not a field guess.

nec2023_change.change: Section 409.60 for industrial control panels was restructured, creating (A) Grounding and (B) Bonding.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 409.60 Bonding

nec2023_change.change: New Section 409.70 has been added requiring surge protection for industrial control panels.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 409.70 Surge Protection

sections.why_it_exists: A short circuit does not ask permission. If the fault current at a panel is higher than the panel was built and tested to withstand, the failure is not a tripped breaker — it is bus bars tearing loose, contacts welding, and an enclosure coming apart in front of whoever is standing there. The SCCR marking is the panel's tested ceiling, and the available fault current is the number it has to beat.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is the breaker's interrupting rating: 'The main breaker is rated 22 kA, so the panel is good for 22 kA.' The breaker's AIC is one component's rating. The panel's SCCR is the tested rating of the whole assembly — the weakest part sets it — and 409.110 makes the marked SCCR the number the installation is judged against.

sections.title: Industrial control panels — marking and short-circuit current rating (409.110)
sections.plain_explanation: Article 409 panels — the factory-built control panels that run machinery and HVAC equipment — must be marked under 409.110 with the panel's electrical ratings, and the marking includes the panel's short-circuit current rating (SCCR). The SCCR is a ceiling: the panel may not be installed where the available fault current exceeds it. Read the panel label the way you read a motor nameplate before the panel is set — supply voltage, phases, and SCCR all come off that mark, and a missing or illegible SCCR is a stop-and-ask, not a guess.
sections.on_the_job: On light-commercial equipment swaps, photograph the control panel label with the rest of the nameplates. If the new panel's SCCR is lower than what the service can deliver, that is an engineering conversation before the panel is set, not after.

sections.title: Luminaires, lampholders, and lamps — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 410 covers light fixtures in the broad code sense: luminaires, lampholders, and lamps — where they may be installed, how they are supported, temperature limits near combustible material, and the special zones in bathtubs, showers, and clothes closets. The parts Sharma hits constantly:
• The tub and shower zone (410.10(D)): 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of the tub rim or the shower threshold. Inside it, a luminaire must be listed for damp locations, and for wet locations where shower spray hits it. Pendants, hanging fixtures, and ceiling-suspended fans are not permitted in the zone at all.
• Clothes closets (410.16): clearances are measured from the closet storage space — 12 in for a surface-mounted enclosed incandescent or LED fixture, 6 in for surface fluorescent and for recessed fixtures. Open-lamp incandescent fixtures and pendants are not permitted at any clearance.
• Recessed fixtures: insulation contact and thermal protection (410.116).
Fixture listing and its instructions (110.3(B)) do half the work in this article — the box and the spec sheet are part of the code answer.
sections.on_the_job: Read the fixture's own listing before you rough the box: weight, temperature rating, damp/wet rating, and closet or shower suitability are all on the label or the cut sheet, not in the field manual. On a Florida master bath, mark the 3 ft by 8 ft zone on the plan at rough-in: the architect's shower light inside it must be the listed wet-location model, and the vanity fixtures sit outside the zone. In the closet, default to an enclosed LED fixture, surface-mounted at 12 in clear of the storage space — never a pendant or an exposed lamp.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma bath practice (company practice, not 410): vanity lighting plus the architect's wet-location shower light, with no extra general ceiling light added by habit. Follow the plan; do not add or delete bath lights on your own.

The rule also now spells out which cords trigger it. Grow lights on a circuit over 150 volts to ground, such as 277 volts from a 480Y/277 system, must be protected by a listed SPGFCI.

The zone and clearance rules keep hot lamps off combustibles and keep the wrong fixture types out of reach of a person in a tub.

The second trap is measuring closet clearances from the wall or the clothes instead of from the storage space the Code defines.

sections.title: Luminaires in the bathtub and shower zone
sections.plain_explanation: Section 410.10(D) controls fixtures inside the zone measured 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of the tub rim or the shower threshold. Inside that zone a luminaire must be listed for damp locations, and for wet locations where it is subject to shower spray, and certain fixture types — including hanging fixtures, pendants, and ceiling-suspended fans — are not permitted in the zone at all. A fixture outside the zone is not governed by this subsection even if it is in the same bathroom.
sections.on_the_job: Mark the zone on the plan at rough-in and check every bath fixture against it, including the shower light and any fan/light combo. Confirm the damp or wet marking on the fixture label matches where it actually sits, and keep the label information in the job file.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma note: the architect's specified shower light is the fixture of record — install the listed wet-location model specified, not a damp-only substitute from stock.

sections.title: Luminaires in clothes closets — permitted types and clearances
sections.plain_explanation: Section 410.16 controls what may light a clothes closet and how far it must sit from the closet storage space — the volume defined in 410.2: 24 inches out from the side and back walls, from the floor up to 6 feet or the highest clothes-hanging rod, and 12 inches out from the walls, or the width of the shelf if greater, from there up to the ceiling. Permitted types [410.16(A)]: surface-mounted or recessed incandescent or LED luminaires with a completely enclosed light source; surface-mounted or recessed fluorescent luminaires; and surface-mounted fluorescent or LED luminaires identified as suitable for installation within the closet storage space. Not permitted [410.16(B)]: incandescent luminaires with open or partially enclosed lamps, and pendant luminaires or lampholders. Minimum clearances from the nearest point of the storage space [410.16(C)]: 12 inches for a surface-mounted incandescent or LED luminaire with a completely enclosed light source, installed on the ceiling or the wall above the door; 6 inches for a surface-mounted fluorescent luminaire in the same positions; 6 inches for a recessed incandescent or LED luminaire with a completely enclosed light source; and 6 inches for a recessed fluorescent luminaire. A surface-mounted fluorescent or LED luminaire identified for use within the closet storage space may be installed inside the storage space itself [410.16(C)(5)].
sections.on_the_job: Measure the clearance from the storage space, not from the wall or the clothes — that 24-inch and 12-inch volume exists on paper even in an empty closet. Default habit: an enclosed LED fixture, surface-mounted at 12 inches clear of the storage space or recessed at 6 inches, and never a pendant or an exposed lamp in a closet.

sections.title: Recessed luminaires — insulation contact and thermal protection
sections.plain_explanation: Section 410.116 covers recessed luminaires: the clearance they must keep from combustible material, the thermal protection that shuts the fixture down if it overheats, and the difference between fixtures listed for direct contact with insulation (Type IC) and those that must keep insulation away. An IC rating is a property of the specific fixture, not of recessed fixtures in general. The fixture's marking also decides whether it may be installed in a ceiling that will be insulated after the fact.
sections.on_the_job: Read the housing label before the ceiling closes: IC or non-IC, and the insulation clearance if it is non-IC. In an insulated Florida attic ceiling, a non-IC can buried in blown insulation is both a code correction and a heat problem — flag it at rough-in, while the fix is still cheap.

sections.title: Lighting systems operating at 30 volts or less — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 411 covers lighting systems operating at 30 volts AC or 60 volts DC or less — and only 15 volts AC or 30 volts DC where contact with water is likely. It covers the listed system as a package: the power supply, the fixtures, and the secondary wiring between them.
• Listed system: the system is installed as a listed assembly — a complete listed system, or one assembled from listed parts (411.4). Loose parts gathered in the field do not make an Article 411 system.
• Power supply: the listed power source limits the secondary circuit — the article caps secondary output at 25 amperes.
• Secondary wiring: the conductors on the load side of the power supply follow Article 411's own rules, not ordinary branch-circuit wiring rules.
• Locations: bare-conductor systems are not concealed and do not run through walls, floors or ceilings unless the specific listed system permits it, and the secondary wiring stays out of the pool zone — not within 10 ft of pools, spas, fountains or similar locations unless Article 680 permits it (411.5).
Sharma meets this article mainly in landscape-style and specialty accent lighting inside a project.
sections.on_the_job: A Lake Nona lanai job: the owner wants 24 V DC LED accent lighting around a covered patio that sits near the pool. Spec the listed system — the manufacturer's listed driver, cable and fixtures as one family. The driver is rated 100 W at 24 V DC; the tape and puck runs total 72 W, inside the rating. Route the secondary so the nearest fixture stays 12 ft from the pool water — outside the 10 ft limit in 411.5 — and keep the driver accessible in the garage, not buried in the soffit.
sections.why_it_exists: Thirty volts sounds harmless, so these systems get treated like doorbell wire. But a secondary that can deliver up to 25 amperes will heat a bad splice or an undersized conductor until something chars. The listing is the protection: the power supply, cable and fixtures were tested together, with the supply limiting what a fault can draw. Field-assembled parts have no tested limit.
inspection_fails: Unlisted power supply and tape installed as a 'system' — no listing for the assembly (411.4).
Secondary conductors concealed in the wall with no listed system permitting it (411.5).
Low-voltage fixtures within 10 ft of pool water with no Article 680 basis (411.5).
Secondary splices buried in mulch or underground where the listing does not allow them.
Power supply inaccessible — sealed above a closed soffit.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is '30 volts or less means wire it like a doorbell — any parts, any method.' An Article 411 system is a listed system: a random driver and a roll of tape bought online is not one, no matter how low the voltage. The second trap is the pool: within 10 ft of the water the location rules bite, and where contact with water is likely the ceiling drops to 15 volts AC or 30 volts DC.

sections.title: Low-voltage lighting systems — where they may and may not go (Article 411)
sections.plain_explanation: Article 411 covers lighting systems operating at not more than 30 volts AC or 60 volts DC (411.1, 2020) — the listed low-voltage systems behind a lot of LED tape, under-cabinet, and accent work. The system must be listed as a complete system or assembled from listed parts, the power source limits the secondary circuit (the article caps secondary output at 25 amperes), and the bare-conductor versions carry location limits: not concealed or run through walls, floors, or ceilings unless the specific listed system permits it, and kept clear of pools, spas, and similar locations except as the article allows. A loose power supply and a roll of tape bought online is not an Article 411 system. Location limits are 411.5: not concealed or extended through a building wall, floor or ceiling unless wired with a Chapter 3 method or Class 2 wiring where the power supply is Class 2, and not within 10 ft of pools, spas, fountains or similar locations unless Article 680 permits. 411.4 itself is the listing rule (a complete listed system, or assembled from listed parts).
sections.on_the_job: Spec the listed system — power supply, cable, and fixtures from one listed family — and keep the driver accessible. Inspectors ask whose system it is; 'the homeowner bought it online' is not an answer.

sections.title: Appliances — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 422 covers appliances: water heaters, dishwashers, disposals, ranges and cooktops, dryers as appliances, space heaters that plug or hard-wire as appliances, and similar equipment. Its working parts:
• Branch-circuit sizing from the appliance's marked rating; an individual branch circuit — one appliance only — is the default for the big fixed appliances (422.10).
• Overcurrent protection: where the appliance is marked with a maximum overcurrent device, the marking governs. An unmarked single non-motor appliance rated over 13.3 A may be protected at up to 150 percent of its rating (422.11(E)).
• Storage water heaters of 120 gallons or less: the branch circuit is sized at 125 percent of the nameplate — a continuous load (422.13).
• GFCI protection that travels with the appliance, wherever it is installed: dishwashers, sump pumps, vending machines, and the rest of the 422.5(A) list.
• A disconnecting means that lets a servicer kill the appliance safely (422.31).
Where an appliance is also a motor load or also HVAC equipment, Articles 430 and 440 may govern instead or in addition — check the appliance's own article first.
sections.on_the_job: For every appliance on a job, settle three things from the nameplate before rough-in is closed: circuit size, cord-and-plug or hard-wired, and where the disconnect will be. The nameplate, not the catalog photo, is the source. Worked example, the standard Florida water heater: 4,500 W at 240 V draws 18.75 A; at 125 percent that is 23.4 A, so it lands on a 30 A circuit with 10 AWG copper. The dishwasher gets its GFCI protection because 422.5 names the appliance — on Sharma work the dual-function breaker supplies it. The microwave gets its own 20 A circuit (S-06).
sections.sharma_note: S-06 is PENDING. The microwave gets its own 20A circuit and is not lumped onto a circuit shared with the hood or anything else. The wire (12 AWG copper versus 10 AWG CCA) is not settled until Mike Holt rules.

sections.why_it_exists: Appliances are the loads that run unattended — a water heater recovering a tank at 3 a.m., a dishwasher cycling while the house is empty. Sized wrong, the circuit cooks slowly inside a wall; serviced without a disconnect, the appliance stays live in the tech's hands. The article ties circuit, protection, and disconnect to the one document that knows the load: the nameplate.

The 4,500 W heater's 18.75 A becomes a 23.4 A minimum, so the 20 A answer fails before the breaker is even picked.
