sections.title: GFCI protection required for specific appliances
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 422.5 names the appliances that must have Class A GFCI protection for personnel wherever they are installed — the duty travels with the appliance, on top of the room rules in 210.8, and meeting one does not erase the other. The 2020 list at 422.5(A) is: automotive vacuum machines; drinking water coolers and bottle fill stations; cord-and-plug-connected high-pressure spray washing machines; tire inflation machines; vending machines; sump pumps; and dishwashers. It reaches appliances rated 150 volts or less to ground and 60 amperes or less, single- or 3-phase, cord-and-plug-connected or hardwired, and 210.8(D) points to this same list. The protection must be readily accessible and provided by one of the methods 422.5(B) permits — a GFCI breaker, a GFCI receptacle, or another listed point the section allows. Edition caution: wider appliance lists circulating from NEC 2023 research are not the 2020 list — in 2020, ranges, dryers, and microwaves pick up their GFCI duties through the location rules in 210.8, not through 422.5. NEC 2020 removed the 'provided for public use' condition and added sump pumps. 422.5(B) locations: the branch-circuit overcurrent device; a device or outlet within the supply circuit; an integral part of the attachment plug; within the supply cord not more than 12 in. from the attachment plug; or factory-installed within the appliance.

sections.title: Branch circuits for appliances (422.10)
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 422.10 starts appliance work with the circuit: the branch circuit must be sized for the appliance it serves, using the appliance's marked rating, and an individual branch circuit — one that supplies only that appliance — is the default pattern for the big fixed appliances. Where two or more appliances share a circuit, this section's load rules and the general rules of Articles 210 and 220 both apply. The numbers that ride with it:
• Where the appliance is marked with a maximum overcurrent device, the marking governs (422.11)
• A single non-motor appliance rated over 13.3 A, not marked with a maximum, may be protected at up to 150 percent of its rating; at 13.3 A or less the ceiling is 20 A (422.11(E))
• A fixed storage water heater of 120 gallons or less is sized at 125 percent of nameplate — a continuous load (422.13)
When the nameplate and the circuit disagree, the circuit gets corrected; the appliance does not get derated by hope.
sections.on_the_job: Takeoff habit: every fixed appliance on the plans gets a line — appliance, rating, circuit, disconnect. If a plan shows the appliance but no circuit home, that is an open question for the packet, not a field surprise. Worked line: a 4,500 W storage water heater at 240 V draws 18.75 A; as a continuous load under 422.13 the circuit is sized at 125 percent — 23.4 A minimum — so the line reads: water heater, 18.75 A, 30 A circuit on 10 AWG copper, lockable disconnect. Every fixed appliance on the plan gets the same four boxes filled before the packet goes out.
sections.figure_idea: Takeoff worksheet strip: appliance, rating, circuit, disconnect — four boxes in a row.
sections.why_it_exists: An appliance is a known, fixed load that runs exactly as hard as its nameplate says, sometimes for hours. A circuit sized by habit instead of by the rating either nuisance-trips under a load that was never a fault, or leaves conductors and terminations carrying more than they were built for. Starting from the marked rating is what keeps both the appliance and the circuit honest.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is protecting an unmarked 16 A appliance with a 20 A breaker 'because it fits.' Section 422.11(E) works the other way: over 13.3 A with no marked maximum, the ceiling is 150 percent of the appliance rating — the breaker follows the appliance, not the other way around. The other common miss is sizing the storage water heater at 100 percent; at 120 gallons or less it is a continuous load at 125 percent (422.13).

Unmarked appliance over 13.3 A protected above 150 percent of its rating (422.11(E)).
Storage water heater of 120 gallons or less wired at 100 percent instead of 125 percent (422.13).
Fixed appliance on the plans with no circuit assigned — found in the field, not on the takeoff.

sections.title: Overcurrent protection for appliances (422.11)
sections.plain_explanation: Section 422.11 protects the appliance at the size the appliance was built for. Where the appliance is marked with a maximum overcurrent device, that marking governs. For a single non-motor appliance fastened in place and rated over 13.3 amperes, where the appliance is not marked with a maximum OCPD: 20A maximum if the appliance is rated 13.3A or less; 150% of the rated current maximum if rated over 13.3A, and where 150% does not land on a standard rating the next higher standard size is permitted (422.11(E)). — a ceiling, not a target. Motor-operated appliances follow the motor rules for their protection, and infrared heating appliances carry their own subdivision limits in this section. 422.11(F): resistance-type heating elements in electric heating appliances rated over 48A must be subdivided, each subdivided load not over 48A and protected at not more than 60A.
sections.on_the_job: Read the appliance label before the breaker is chosen, every time. 'It matched the panel schedule from the last job' is how a 50 A device lands on an appliance marked 30 A maximum.

sections.title: Storage water heaters — treat the load as continuous for circuit sizing
sections.plain_explanation: Section 422.13 sizes the branch circuit for a fixed storage water heater of 120 gallons or less at not less than 125 percent of the heater's nameplate rating. In practice that is why a common 4500W, 240V heater (18.75A) lands on a 25A minimum calculation and is conventionally wired on a 30A circuit with 10 AWG copper — the arithmetic must be run for the actual nameplate on the actual job, not copied from the last house. The heater is treated this way because it can run for long stretches recovering a tank.
sections.on_the_job:
Do the division every time: nameplate watts divided by voltage, times 1.25, then choose the standard breaker and conductor that cover it. Write the result on the panel schedule so the next person does not have to reverse-engineer it.

Worked example: a 5,500 W, 240 V heater draws 5,500 ÷ 240 = 22.9 A; × 1.25 = 28.6 A minimum circuit — a 30A breaker on 10 AWG copper covers it. The standard 4,500 W heater works out to 18.75 A × 1.25 = 23.4 A, which is why it also lands on the same 30A / 10 AWG circuit.

sections.title: Cord-and-plug connection for range hoods
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 422.16(B)(4) lets a listed range hood — and an over-the-range microwave/range hood combination — be cord-and-plug connected instead of hard-wired, but only when every condition in the subsection is met:
• The flexible cord is identified as suitable for use on range hoods in the manufacturer's installation instructions.
• The cord is not less than 18 in. and not over 4 ft long.
• The cord has an equipment grounding conductor and ends in a grounding-type attachment plug. Exception: a listed hood marked as double-insulated does not need the grounding-type plug.
• The receptacle is located so the cord is protected against physical damage.
• The receptacle is accessible.
• The receptacle is supplied by an individual branch circuit.
Cord connection is what lets the hood come down for service without unwiring it. It is a listed, conditioned permission — not a general shortcut for any fixed appliance.
sections.on_the_job: Marion Oaks kitchen: the plan shows an over-the-range microwave/hood combination. Under S-06 it gets its own dedicated 20 A circuit — never shared. The receptacle goes in the cabinet above the unit, where the cord reaches it without crossing the cooktop: the factory cord is 24 in., inside the 18 in. to 4 ft window. Before rough-in, confirm the unit's instructions identify the cord for range hood use; a hood listed for hard-wiring only gets hard-wired, cord kit or not.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma note (company practice, not a 422 rule): the range hood often rides the dishwasher/disposal circuit in Sharma design practice. S-06 still stands on its own — the microwave keeps its own dedicated 20A circuit and is never lumped in with the hood. The wire size on that circuit is PENDING (12 AWG copper versus 10 AWG CCA).
sections.why_it_exists: Hoods live over a hot cooktop in grease-laden air, and they come down for cleaning and service more than almost any other fixed appliance. The cord makes that practical. The conditions keep the cord itself from becoming the hazard: short enough to stay off the burners, grounded, protected from damage, and on its own circuit so the hood is not sharing a loaded kitchen circuit.
inspection_fails: Cord-and-plug hood receptacle fed from the small-appliance or dishwasher circuit — not an individual branch circuit.
Hood cord 5 ft long, draped behind the range to reach a receptacle.
Receptacle hidden behind the hood's duct cover — not accessible.
Cord kit added to a hood whose instructions list it for hard-wiring only.
Receptacle located where a cabinet door or the duct pinches the cord.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating cord connection as permission to plug the hood into any handy receptacle — the countertop small-appliance circuit, or the dishwasher/disposal circuit. For a cord-and-plug hood, 422.16(B)(4) requires an individual branch circuit. The other trap is the cord length: over 4 ft fails, even if everything else is right.

sections.title: Disconnecting means for permanently connected appliances
sections.plain_explanation: Section 422.31 covers how a permanently connected appliance is disconnected for service. Depending on the appliance's rating, the disconnect may be a switch or breaker that meets the article's conditions, and for larger appliances the disconnect must be capable of being locked in the open position or meet the subsection that applies to its size. The intent is simple: the person servicing the appliance must be able to cut its power and keep it cut. The branch-circuit breaker can serve this role only where the conditions for doing so are met.
sections.on_the_job: At rough-in, decide where each hard-wired appliance's disconnect lives and confirm a servicer can reach it. A water heater, an air handler, or a cooktop whose only disconnect is an unlabelled breaker two rooms away is a conversation to have before final, not after.

sections.title: Fixed electric space-heating equipment — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 424 covers heating that is built into the building: baseboard heaters, wall heaters, radiant panels and cables, duct heaters, and boilers used for space heat. Its core ideas are that heating loads are treated as continuous, that the equipment must be listed and installed to its instructions, and that disconnects and controls must let the heater be serviced and shut off safely. In Florida houses Sharma meets this article most often at duct heat strips in an air handler and at the occasional wall or bath heater.

Heating cable can now go in, on or behind a wall when the cable or cable set is identified for wall use.
• 424.10: Section 424.10, Special Permission, was deleted, and 424.9, General, was relocated to 424.10 at the beginning of Article 424 Part II.
• 424.93(C): This new first-level subdivision created will allow heating panels and heating panel sets to be installed in walls with specific protection and limitations. The provision includes a January 1, 2026, effective date.

sections.title: Branch circuits for fixed electric space heating (424.4(A), 424.4(B))
sections.plain_explanation: Fixed electric space heating — baseboard, wall heaters, ceiling heat, and the electric heat built into equipment — is served by individual branch circuits under 424.4(A), with the central systems the article names as the exception pattern. Under 424.4(B) the heating load is treated as continuous: branch-circuit conductors and overcurrent protection are sized at 125 percent of the total heating load on the circuit, before any other load is considered. A heater is not a convenience load that happens to get warm; it runs for hours at full draw. Circuits supplying two or more heater outlets are rated 15, 20, 25 or 30A; in other than dwelling units, fixed infrared heating may be on circuits up to 50A (424.4(A)). (424.3(A)/(B) are the 2017 numbers.)
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: a 4,800 W, 240 V wall heater draws 20 A. Continuous sizing makes the circuit 20 × 1.25 = 25 A — so the circuit is built at 25 A or above, never the 20 A circuit the raw math suggests.
sections.figure_idea: One heater, two math lines: nameplate amps, then the 125 percent continuous line landing on the breaker size.

sections.title: Branch-circuit sizing for fixed space heat — 125 percent
sections.plain_explanation: Section 424.4(B) is where this rule lives in the 2020 edition — it was 424.3(B) in 2017, before the Article 424 reorganization. The 2020 text states the sizing directly instead of using the old 'shall be considered continuous load' sentence: the branch-circuit conductors for fixed electric space-heating equipment and any associated motors shall be sized not smaller than 125 percent of the load. Overcurrent protection is sized at the same 125 percent through the continuous-load rules of 210.19(A)(1) and 210.20(A), so in practice both the conductors and the breaker come out at 125 percent of the total load connected to the circuit, heater plus any blower or fan motor in the same equipment.
sections.on_the_job:
Run the math at 125 percent: total nameplate amps, heater plus motor, times 1.25 — then select the conductor and the breaker.

Worked example: a 10 kW duct heater at 240 V draws 41.7 A; × 1.25 = 52.1 A — conductors rated at least 52.1 A (6 AWG copper at the 75°C column gives 65 A) on a 60A breaker, and the blower motor amps in the same equipment are added to the heater amps before the 125 percent is applied.

sections.title: Disconnecting means for fixed space-heating equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 424.19 requires a disconnecting means for fixed electric space-heating equipment — baseboard and wall heaters, duct heaters, and heat strips in an air handler. One operation has to kill the whole machine:
• The disconnect must simultaneously disconnect the heater, the motor controller(s) and any supplementary overcurrent protective device(s) from all ungrounded conductors.
• It must be lockable in the open position under 110.25 — the locking provision is part of the switch or breaker and stays in place with or without the lock.
• The disconnect must have an ampere rating not less than 125 percent of the total load of the motors and the heaters.
• Equipment with supplementary overcurrent protection: the disconnect is within sight from those devices — visible and not more than 50 ft away.
• Equipment without supplementary overcurrent protection: the branch-circuit switch or breaker may serve as the disconnect, if it is within sight from the heater or lockable under 110.25 [424.19(B)].
• A unit switch that is part of the equipment, with a marked "off" position, may serve as the disconnect where it disconnects all ungrounded conductors [424.19(C)].
A duct heater in an air handler is normally disconnected at the air handler's disconnect — the 440/424 boundary matters on a change-out, because the strips and the blower are one piece of equipment at service time.
sections.on_the_job: Air-handler change-out in a Florida garage: the new unit carries 10 kW of strip heat and a blower, fed as one piece of equipment. The disconnect at the air handler must kill the strips, the blower and the controller together — test all three dead before your hands go in. The strip circuit is sized at 125 percent under 424.4(B): 10 kW at 240 V is 41.7 A — 52.1 A minimum, 60 A breaker. If you move the disconnect on the change-out, re-verify at the new location that it still opens the whole unit, and check the heat-strip circuit before start-up. Keep the disconnect within reach of the person servicing the unit.
sections.why_it_exists: Heat strips and a blower share one cabinet, and the tech services them with the cabinet open and both hands inside. If the switch he opened kills the strips but leaves the blower or the controls live — or someone resets a breaker down the hall mid-repair — the "dead" unit starts or bites. One disconnect that opens everything and locks open is what makes the equipment safe to open up.
inspection_fails: Disconnect opens the heat strips but the blower and controls stay live — it must open the heater, the controller and the supplementary protection together.
Out-of-sight disconnect with no lockable provision, or a portable hasp clipped on — 110.25 requires the provision to stay in place with or without the lock.
Unit has supplementary fuses inside, and the disconnect is around the corner, out of sight from those devices.
Unit switch used as the disconnect with no marked "off" position, or it opens only one ungrounded conductor.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is "the panel breaker is the disconnect, full stop." That only works for equipment without supplementary overcurrent protection, and only when the breaker is within sight of the heater or lockable under 110.25. If the unit carries its own supplementary fuses or breakers, the disconnect must be within sight from those devices.

sections.title: Fixed resistance and electrode industrial process heating equipment — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 425 covers electric heating used for an industrial process rather than for comfort: process tanks, ovens, and similar equipment.
• The article follows the use, not the hardware: the same heating element is 424 work when it warms people and 425 work when it heats a product.
• Sharma's residential and light commercial work rarely installs it, so this page is the article's scope page.
• Where a commercial job includes process heat, work the article with the equipment listing, and ask Mike before treating it like space heat under 424.
sections.on_the_job: Do not borrow 424 rules for a 425 load by habit. Identify the article from the equipment's use, then apply that article plus the listing. Example: a small commercial job adds an electric process tank heater. Before quoting, get the nameplate and the listing instructions, confirm which article the job falls under, and let Mike review the plan: the wire and protection follow 425 and the listing, not the duct-heater job from last week.

sections.title: Fixed outdoor electric deicing and snow-melting equipment — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 426 covers fixed electric equipment installed outdoors to melt snow and ice: heating cable and panels in pavements, walks, driveways, roofs and gutters. It is a later-pass article for a Florida book — Sharma does not install snow-melting in its territory — and it is included here so Chapter 4 walks the NEC in complete official order. The rules that do the work when this equipment appears:
• Continuous load (426.4): branch-circuit conductors and the overcurrent device are sized at not less than 125 percent of the total heater load.
• Ground-fault protection of equipment (426.28): GFPE must be provided for the equipment, except for mineral-insulated, metal-sheathed cable embedded in a noncombustible medium. GFPE protects equipment — it is not a personnel GFCI.
• Disconnecting means (426.50): a means that disconnects all ungrounded conductors at the same time, capable of being locked open.
• Identification (426.13): the presence of a deicing or snow-melting installation must be indicated, so nobody cores or cuts into a heated slab blind.
sections.on_the_job: If a Florida job somehow specifies deicing equipment — a northern builder's standard detail copied onto a Florida plan is the usual way — flag it to the office rather than installing or deleting it silently. If the office ever approves one, the math looks like this: a 2,400 W heated walk on 240 V draws 10 A; treated as the continuous load it is, the circuit sizes at 125 percent, 12.5 A, so a 15 A breaker is the smallest standard pick — and it must be a GFPE breaker, not a standard one (426.28).
sections.florida_note: Florida note: no snow load in Sharma's territory; treat any 426 equipment on a Florida plan as a probable copy-over from another climate and confirm with the builder.

sections.title: Fixed electric heating equipment for pipelines and vessels — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 427 covers fixed electric heating equipment for pipelines and vessels: heat-tracing cable and heating panels that keep a pipe from freezing or hold a process fluid at temperature.
• Scope: the heating cable or panel, its controls and its branch circuit (427.1).
• The load is continuous: branch-circuit conductors and overcurrent protection are sized at 125 percent of the total heating load (427.4).
• Ground-fault protection of equipment is required on the branch circuits that supply heat tracing and heating panels (427.22). It is equipment protection, commonly a 30 mA trip — not a 4–6 mA personnel GFCI. A narrow exception covers industrial plants with alarm indication and qualified maintenance.
• Heating cables carry a grounded conductive covering: the metal braid or jacket is the fault path that lets the protection see a failure (427.23).
• Caution signs or markings go on the pipe or vessel at intervals of not more than 20 ft, and next to equipment that gets serviced (427.13).
• Each installation has a disconnecting means that opens all ungrounded conductors (427.55(A)).
Sharma meets this article as pipe heat trace on exposed commercial plumbing and in freeze protection details, not in ordinary house work.
sections.on_the_job: A small commercial building in Ocala has 40 ft of exposed domestic water pipe and a backflow preventer in an unconditioned meter room. Sharma installs self-regulating heat trace under the pipe insulation, fed from a 20 A GFPE breaker — Sharma's commercial minimum branch circuit is 20 A. The cable load is 8 A; figured as a continuous load at 125 percent, that is 10 A, well inside the circuit. Caution markings go on the pipe at 20 ft intervals and at the valve that gets serviced. Install the heat trace exactly to its listing: correct cable for the pipe, correct controller and sensor location, GFPE in place and tested. Photograph the controller setting at turnover.

sections.why_it_exists: A heat-trace cable lives outdoors, under insulation, wrapped on a pipe full of water. When its insulation fails, the fault can arc and sputter without ever drawing enough current to trip a plain breaker — heating the pipe covering instead. GFPE watches for that small leak to ground and opens the circuit, and the grounded braid gives the fault a path the protection can see. The caution signs warn the next trade off a live cable hidden under insulation.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is reaching for a Class A GFCI. Section 427.22 asks for ground-fault protection of equipment, which trips around 30 mA to catch a failing cable; a 4–6 mA personnel GFCI is a different device that nuisance-trips on long runs. Second trap: sizing the branch circuit at 100 percent of the cable load — heating is a continuous load and takes 125 percent (427.4).

Cable installed without its grounded conductive covering, or the braid left ungrounded at the termination (427.23).
Branch circuit sized at 100 percent of the heating load — a continuous load takes 125 percent (427.4).
Controller sensor hanging in the air instead of strapped to the pipe, so the cable cooks the covering or the pipe freezes.

sections.title: Motors, motor circuits, and controllers — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 430 is the longest working article in Chapter 4 and the one most often misapplied, because it is a system, not a single rule: conductors sized from table full-load current, separate overload protection sized from the nameplate, short-circuit and ground-fault protection sized from its own tables and percentages, a controller, and a disconnect within sight. Each of those five jobs has its own sizing basis, and using one number for all five is the classic 430 error. Air-conditioning equipment is pulled out of parts of 430 by Article 440, which has its own nameplate-driven rules — always check which article governs the equipment in front of you.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 430.2: Rebuilt motors now have a home in 430.2: they're allowed when the work follows the manufacturer's instructions, or a nationally recognized standard if the maker offers none. A reconditioned motor can go back into service when the rebuild followed the manufacturer's instructions.
• 430.1: The previous figure at Section 430.1 has been deleted, and an expanded figure has been added to include all relevant parts of the motor circuit and what parts of Article 430 apply.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Work a motor in this order, every time: (1) table FLC for conductors and short-circuit protection, (2) nameplate FLA for overloads, (3) disconnect within sight, (4) controller rating. Write all four down before you order material.

sections.title: Which current do you size from — table values vs. nameplate
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 430.6 is the traffic rule for the whole article. For sizing conductors, disconnects, controllers, and short-circuit/ground-fault protection, you use the full-load current values from the Article 430 tables for the motor's horsepower and voltage — not the amps printed on that particular motor's nameplate, because the next replacement motor may differ. Overload protection is the exception: it is sized from the actual nameplate current of the motor installed, because it protects that specific machine. Mixing those two bases up is the single most common motor calculation error.

Table values the crews use most — single-phase from Table 430.248, three-phase from Table 430.250:
• 1/2 hp, 115 V — 9.8 A
• 1 hp, 115 V — 16 A
• 1 hp, 230 V — 8 A
• 2 hp, 230 V — 12 A
• 3 hp, 230 V — 17 A
• 5 hp, 230 V — 28 A
• 1 hp, 208 V, 3-phase — 4.6 A
• 5 hp, 208 V, 3-phase — 16.7 A
• 10 hp, 208 V, 3-phase — 30.8 A
• 10 hp, 460 V, 3-phase — 14 A
The fuller table is on the 430.250 page. If the horsepower and voltage in front of you are not listed here, pull the value from the printed table for that combination — do not scale from a nearby row.
sections.on_the_job: Keep two numbers on your worksheet and label them: 'Table FLC' and 'Nameplate FLA.' If a number on your page is not labelled, stop and label it before you size anything from it.

sections.title: Conductors for a single motor — 125 percent of table full-load current
sections.plain_explanation: Section 430.22 sizes the branch-circuit conductors feeding one continuous-duty motor at not less than 125 percent of the motor's full-load current as taken from the Article 430 tables. The extra quarter covers the heating of a motor that runs for long periods at full load. Intermittent and short-time duty motors are treated under their own parts of this section, so the duty rating on the nameplate decides which rule you are in before you do any arithmetic.
sections.on_the_job:
Take the table FLC for the horsepower and voltage, multiply by 1.25, then select the conductor from the ampacity table using the correct temperature column for the terminations. Do not size the wire from the nameplate amps and do not round the 125 percent away.

Worked example: a 5 hp, 230 V single-phase motor has a table FLC of 28 A (Table 430.248). Conductors: 28 × 1.25 = 35 A minimum — 10 AWG copper at the 75°C column (35 A) is the smallest conductor that covers it, before any voltage-drop or adjustment checks.

sections.title: Conductors feeding several motors
sections.plain_explanation: Section 430.24 sizes conductors that feed two or more motors (or motors with other loads): take 125 percent of the full-load current of the largest motor, add the full-load currents of the other motors at 100 percent, and add any other loads under their own rules, all using the Article 430 table values. The largest motor gets the continuous-duty margin; the rest are added at face value, on the reasonable basis that the feeder sees the sum. It is the feeder-level companion to the single-motor rule in 430.22.
sections.on_the_job: Build the sum in a labelled column — largest motor first at 125 percent, then each additional motor at 100 percent — so the next person can audit it. Do not apply 125 percent to every motor on the feeder, and do not size a multi-motor feeder from one nameplate.

sections.title: Overload protection — protects the motor from running too hot
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 430.32 requires overload protection for continuous-duty motors over the small sizes the article sets, sized from the motor's nameplate full-load current with the percentage depending on the motor's service factor and temperature-rise markings. The overload device watches running current over time and trips before the windings cook; it is not there to clear a short circuit, which is the branch protective device's job. A motor with built-in thermal protection meets this requirement through its own device where the article allows it.

The percentages in 430.32(A)(1), applied to the nameplate full-load current:
• Motor with a marked service factor of 1.15 or greater — 125 percent
• Motor with a marked temperature rise of 40°C or less — 125 percent
• All other motors — 115 percent
If an overload selected at those percentages will not let the motor start or carry its load, 430.32(C) permits stepping up — to not more than 140 percent for the first two cases, 130 percent for all others. The step-up is a documented exception for a motor that will not run, not the starting point for selection.
sections.on_the_job: Read service factor and rise off the nameplate before you select or set an overload. If the overload trips repeatedly, measure the running amps and find the mechanical cause — do not solve a tripping overload by setting it higher than 430.32 permits.

sections.title: Branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protection for motors
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 430.52 sizes the device that clears a fault on a motor branch circuit, using the percentages in Table 430.52 applied to the table full-load current, with the device type (fuses, inverse-time breaker, instantaneous-trip breaker, and so on) deciding which column applies. These percentages are deliberately far above running current, because the device must ride through motor starting inrush without opening, while still clearing a fault. That is why a motor circuit can legally have a breaker that looks oversized for its wire — the overload device, not the breaker, is protecting the motor and, through its sizing rules, the circuit against overload.

Table 430.52 maximum ratings, as a percentage of table full-load current:
• Nontime-delay (single-element) fuses — 300 percent
• Dual-element (time-delay) fuses — 175 percent
• Inverse-time circuit breakers — 250 percent
• Instantaneous-trip breakers — 800 percent (1100 percent for Design B energy-efficient motors); 430.52(C)(3) Exception No. 1 permits up to 1300 percent where the 800% setting won't let the motor start, and Design B energy-efficient premium motors may go up to 1700 percent
Worked example: the 5 hp, 230 V motor at 28 A table FLC takes an inverse-time breaker of at most 28 × 2.50 = 70 A. If that device will not hold through starting, 430.52(C)(1) Exception No. 2(c) permits an inverse-time breaker up to 400 percent where the FLC is 100 A or less — an exception to document, not a habit. (Exception No. 1 is the next-higher-standard-size permission, for where the table percentage does not land on a standard rating.)
sections.on_the_job: Never judge a motor circuit by house-circuit instincts. Check all three together: conductor at 125 percent of table FLC (430.22), overload from the nameplate (430.32), fault protection from Table 430.52. If one of the three is missing from the job paperwork, the calculation is not finished.

sections.title: Feeder protection where several motors share a feeder (430.62)
sections.plain_explanation: When one feeder supplies several motor branch circuits, 430.62(A) caps the feeder's protective device: no larger than the largest branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault device on the feeder, plus the full-load currents of the other motors on that feeder. The feeder conductors themselves are sized under 430.24 — 125 percent of the largest motor plus 100 percent of the rest. The two rules work as a pair: the wire math keeps the feeder from running hot, and the device math keeps a fault on one motor from being invisible to a feeder breaker sized for everything at once.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: three motors at 14 A, 10 A, and 10 A table FLC, largest branch device 40 A. Feeder device ceiling: 40 + 10 + 10 = 60 A. Feeder conductors: 14 × 1.25 + 10 + 10 = 37.5 A minimum ampacity before other adjustments.

sections.title: The motor disconnect must be within sight
sections.plain_explanation: Section 430.102 places the disconnecting means for a motor and its controller within sight from the equipment it disconnects — visible and not more than 50 ft away, the Article 100 meaning of 'in sight.' The person servicing the machine must be able to see the disconnect, or the disconnect must be of a type that can be locked open under the conditions the article allows. A breaker in a panel across the building, with no lockable arrangement, does not give a servicer control of the machine in front of them.
sections.on_the_job: Stand at the motor and point at its disconnect before you call the job done. If you cannot see it, either move it, add the local disconnect, or confirm the lockable arrangement the article permits and document it. The same within-sight habit is what 440.14 demands for HVAC equipment.

sections.title: What may serve as the motor disconnect
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 430.109 lists the types of switches and devices permitted to serve as a motor disconnect. The general list at 430.109(A):
• A listed motor-circuit switch rated in horsepower
• A listed molded case circuit breaker
• A listed molded case switch
• An instantaneous-trip breaker that is part of a listed combination controller, or a listed self-protected combination controller
• A listed manual motor controller additionally marked 'Suitable as Motor Disconnect,' installed between the final branch-circuit protective device and the motor
Small motors get their own paths. For stationary motors of 1/8 horsepower or less, the branch-circuit overcurrent device may serve as the disconnect (430.109(B)), and cord-and-plug arrangements for small motors sit with 430.111. For stationary motors of 2 horsepower or less and 300 volts or less, a general-use switch rated at not less than twice the motor full-load current is permitted, as is an AC general-use snap switch where the motor current is not more than 80 percent of the switch rating (430.109(C)). A general-use switch that is fine for a lighting load is not automatically a motor disconnect; the device must be rated for interrupting a motor circuit of that horsepower.
sections.on_the_job: Read the horsepower rating on the switch, not just the amp rating, before you land a motor on it. When the disconnect is a breaker in a panelboard, confirm it is a permitted type for that motor and that the within-sight rule in 430.102 is separately satisfied. Small-motor case: a 1/2 hp, 115 V exhaust fan motor has a table full-load current of 9.8 A (Table 430.248). On the 430.109(C) path, a general-use switch rated at least twice that — 19.6 A — serves as the disconnect, so a 20 A switch is the pick; a 15 A lighting toggle is not, whatever is on the truck.
sections.why_it_exists: A motor is not a light bulb. Starting current runs several times the running current, and opening a loaded motor circuit draws an arc the device has to survive thousands of times. A switch chosen by amps alone can weld its contacts or fail closed, leaving a servicer working on a machine that is still alive. The horsepower rating is the proof the device was tested to make and break motor current.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'a 20 A switch for a 20 A motor circuit.' Section 430.109 is a type list, not an amp list: outside the small-motor paths, the disconnect must be a horsepower-rated device or another listed type the section names. The companion trap is forgetting that type is only half the check — 430.110 still sizes the disconnect at not less than 115 percent of the table full-load current, and 430.102 still wants it within sight.
inspection_fails: General-use lighting switch installed as the disconnect for a motor over the small-motor limits, with no horsepower rating.
Manual motor controller used as the disconnect without the 'Suitable as Motor Disconnect' marking (430.109(A)(6)).
Disconnect sized under 115 percent of the motor's table full-load current (430.110).
Permitted device type, but the disconnect is not within sight of the motor (430.102).
General-use switch under twice the full-load current on a 2 hp or less stationary motor (430.109(C)(1)).

sections.title: Rating of the motor disconnect — at least 115 percent
sections.plain_explanation: Section 430.110 sizes the disconnecting means for a motor circuit: a general-use switch used as a motor disconnect must have an ampere rating of at least 115 percent of the motor's full-load current as taken from the Article 430 tables, and horsepower-rated devices are selected by their horsepower rating for the motor served. The disconnect is a switching device that must safely make and break motor current, which is why its sizing basis is its own rule and not simply 'match the breaker.' Combined with 430.102 (within sight) and 430.109 (permitted types), this completes the disconnect picture.
sections.on_the_job: Check two markings on a motor disconnect: the amp rating against 115 percent of table FLC, or the horsepower rating against the motor. If either fails, the disconnect is the wrong device even if it has worked for years on the old motor.

sections.title: Conductors to drives and power conversion equipment (430.122)
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 430.122 sizes the conductors feeding adjustable-speed drives and other power conversion equipment from the equipment's own ratings — not from the motor's horsepower table:
• Supply (input) conductors: ampacity not less than 125 percent of the drive's rated input current [430.122(A)]. The drive nameplate — input amps — is the document that sizes this wire.
• Output conductors, drive to motor: ampacity not less than 125 percent of the motor's full-load current as determined by 430.6 [430.122(B)]. Where the drive is listed and marked "Suitable for Output Motor Conductor Protection," the output conductors must be at least the larger of that 125 percent value or the minimum conductor size marked on the drive.
• Where the equipment has a bypass, the section follows the larger demand — the conductors must suit the bypass arrangement as well as the drive [430.122(C)].
A drive can draw more at its input than the motor table suggests, so both sides of the drive get sized: input from the drive plate, output from the motor.
sections.on_the_job: Swapping a starter for a VFD on a pump or air handler: photograph the drive's input rating before ordering wire. Example: the plate reads INPUT 460 V, 21 A — the supply conductors need an ampacity of at least 21 × 1.25 = 26.25 A, whatever the motor table says. Reusing the old starter's wire size without the input-current check is the standard failure. Check the output side too: drive-to-motor conductors are sized at 125 percent of the motor's full-load current from 430.6.
sections.figure_idea: Nameplate zoom: 'INPUT 460 V 21 A' feeding the 125 percent math line.
sections.why_it_exists: A drive is not a starter. Its input current includes the losses and the harmonic-rich draw of the conversion electronics, and it is set by the drive's rating, not by the motor behind it. Wire sized from the motor table can run hot feeding a drive whose motor is loafing — and a later swap to a larger drive frame on the same motor silently overloads wire that nobody re-checked.
inspection_fails: Drive supply conductors sized from the motor horsepower table instead of the drive's rated input current.
Old starter wire reused on a VFD retrofit with no input-current check.
Output conductors to the motor undersized — not 125 percent of the motor full-load current.
Bypass installed and the conductors never checked for the across-the-line demand.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer sizes the drive's supply conductors from the motor's table full-load current (430.6, 430.22) because "it is a motor circuit." Part X changes the input side: supply conductors come from the drive's rated input current at 125 percent [430.122(A)]. The motor table still governs the output side — not the input.

sections.title: Motor full-load current tables — the working values (430.248 / 430.250)
sections.plain_explanation:
Tables 430.248 (single-phase) and 430.250 (three-phase) are the source of the table full-load current used for conductor, disconnect, controller, and short-circuit sizing under 430.6. The combinations below are the ones Sharma's crews meet most; the printed tables govern for anything not listed here.

Single-phase (Table 430.248):
• 1/2 hp — 9.8 A at 115 V, 4.9 A at 230 V
• 1 hp — 16 A at 115 V, 8 A at 230 V
• 1-1/2 hp — 20 A at 115 V, 10 A at 230 V
• 2 hp — 24 A at 115 V, 12 A at 230 V
• 3 hp — 34 A at 115 V, 17 A at 230 V
• 5 hp — 28 A at 230 V
• 7-1/2 hp — 40 A at 230 V
• 10 hp — 50 A at 230 V

Three-phase (Table 430.250):
• 1 hp — 4.6 A at 208 V, 2.1 A at 460 V
• 3 hp — 10.6 A at 208 V, 4.8 A at 460 V
• 5 hp — 16.7 A at 208 V, 7.6 A at 460 V
• 7-1/2 hp — 24.2 A at 208 V, 11 A at 460 V
• 10 hp — 30.8 A at 208 V, 14 A at 460 V
• 15 hp — 46.2 A at 208 V, 21 A at 460 V
• 20 hp — 59.4 A at 208 V, 27 A at 460 V
• 25 hp — 74.8 A at 208 V, 34 A at 460 V
sections.on_the_job: Keep the two bases separate (430.6): these table numbers size the wire, the disconnect, and the fault protection; the overloads still come off the nameplate of the motor actually installed. A replacement motor of the same horsepower uses the same table FLC even when its nameplate amps differ from the old motor's.

sections.title: Air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 440 takes hermetic refrigerant motor-compressors and air-conditioning equipment out of the general motor rules and gives them a nameplate-driven system. The equipment nameplate states the minimum circuit ampacity (MCA) and the maximum overcurrent protection (MOCP, sometimes marked MOP or 'max fuse/breaker'), and those two printed numbers — not a horsepower table — size the circuit. Article 440 also sets the disconnect rule Sharma's crews use daily: within sight, readily accessible, at the equipment. Where 430 and 440 disagree for a compressor, 440 governs. Florida settles the common condenser question for houses: FBC-Residential §E3408.1 amends 210.8(F) with Exception No. 2 — GFCI protection is not required for listed and labeled HVAC equipment on one- and two-family dwellings.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:

Disconnect readily accessible to unqualified people? A door or hinged cover that opens onto energized parts must need a tool or be lockable.
• 440.8: Section 440.8 now also controls location: A/C and refrigeration equipment can't sit in the zone 3 ft out and 8 ft up, measured from a bathtub's rim or a shower's threshold. Air-conditioning and refrigeration equipment stays out of the zone 3 ft out and 8 ft up, measured from a bathtub's rim or a shower's threshold.

sections.title: Reading the HVAC nameplate — MCA and MOCP do the sizing
sections.plain_explanation: Section 440.4(B) covers the nameplate marking for equipment with a hermetic refrigerant motor-compressor: the plate carries the rated-load current and the branch-circuit selection current, and the manufacturer's marked minimum circuit ampacity and maximum overcurrent device rating are built from them. In field language: MCA tells you the smallest conductor ampacity the circuit may have; MOCP tells you the largest fuse or breaker you may protect it with. A breaker smaller than MOCP is allowed; a conductor smaller than MCA is not. The plate, not a tonnage rule of thumb, is the calculation.
sections.on_the_job:
On every condenser and air handler: record MCA, MOCP, voltage, and phase from the plate. Wire to at least MCA, protect at no more than MOCP, and if the installed breaker or wire disagrees with a change-out unit's new plate, stop and tell the office before start-up — that is a change order conversation, not a field improvisation.

Worked example: a condenser plate reads MCA 24.5 A, MOCP 40 A. The conductor ampacity must be at least 24.5 A — 10 AWG copper (35 A at the 75°C column) covers it — and the breaker may be anything up to 40 A; Sharma's standard install protects it at the MOCP with a standard 2-pole breaker. A same-tonnage change-out plate reading MCA 17.5 / MOCP 30 is a different circuit — the plate, not the tons, decides.
sections.sharma_note: Cross-link (Chapter 2): the question of GFCI protection for outdoor HVAC equipment under 210.8(F) is handled on the Chapter 2 pages and is deliberately not resolved here; local AHJ position governs on the job.

sections.title: Short-circuit current rating of air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment
sections.plain_explanation: Section 440.10 requires motor controllers and industrial control equipment used with air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment to have a short-circuit current rating suitable for the available fault current, with the rating marked as the article requires. It is the Article 440 companion to 408.6 and 409: modern packaged HVAC gear and its control panels carry an SCCR, and a unit installed where the available fault current exceeds it is a mismatch even when MCA and MOCP are perfect. The issue arises on commercial rooftops and larger services, rarely on a house condenser.
sections.on_the_job: On commercial HVAC work, add SCCR to the nameplate photograph set: MCA, MOCP, and SCCR, plus the available fault current when the design provides it. A mismatch goes to Mike before the unit is set, not to the inspector at final.

sections.title: Rating the air-conditioning disconnect (440.12)
sections.plain_explanation:
The disconnecting means for hermetic refrigerant motor-compressor equipment is rated under 440.12, separately from the branch-circuit protection in 440.22. The disconnect's ampere rating must be at least 115 percent of the nameplate rated-load current or the branch-circuit selection current, whichever is greater — or the disconnect may be chosen by the horsepower-equivalent method the section allows. A disconnect that matches the breaker size by habit can still be undersized by this section, because the two devices answer different questions.
• Rating: this page — 115 percent of the greater nameplate current (440.12).
• Location: within sight of the equipment (440.14).
• Protection: the breaker or fuses answer to 440.22 and the nameplate MOCP.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: nameplate rated-load current 28 A. Disconnect minimum: 28 × 1.15 = 32.2 A — so the common 60 A disconnect is the shelf pick, and a 30 A disconnect fails this section even though it exceeds the running amps. Sharma practice at trim: the condenser gets a standard disconnect and whip, set within sight of the unit (440.14) — and the rating still comes from this section, while the breaker follows the nameplate MOCP under 440.22. When a change-out unit's plate shows a higher rated-load current than the old one, re-run the 115 percent before reusing the old disconnect.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma practice (not code): the condenser gets a standard disconnect and whip at trim — the rating still comes from this section, and the breaker follows the nameplate under S-03.

sections.title: The HVAC disconnect — within sight and readily accessible
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 440.14 requires the disconnecting means for air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment to be within sight from the equipment and readily accessible to it, with an exception for certain industrial/process installations where conditions are met. 'Within sight' carries the Article 100 meaning: visible and within 50 ft. The disconnect may be on the equipment or separate from it, but a person servicing the unit must be able to reach it and see the unit from it. A breaker inside the house panel does not satisfy this by itself. The disconnect also may not be mounted on a panel that is designed to allow access to the equipment itself, and it may not be placed where it obscures the equipment nameplate.

• 440.14: The A/C and refrigeration disconnect now has to have 110.26(A) working space, on top of the long-standing in-sight and readily accessible rules. The disconnect for A/C or refrigeration equipment must now have working space that meets 110.26(A).

On a change-out, if the old disconnect is inside the old unit's shadow or was never installed, relocate or add it as part of the job and note it on the invoice record.

sections.title: Short-circuit and ground-fault protection for a compressor circuit
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 440.22 sizes the branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protection for a hermetic motor-compressor circuit and ties it to the equipment's rated-load or branch-circuit selection current, with the marked MOCP on a listed unit's nameplate being the number the installer works to in practice. As with motors generally, this device is allowed to be larger than the conductor's plain ampacity, because equipment overload protection inside the unit does the running protection and the breaker must ride through compressor starting current. That allowance only exists inside Article 440's system — never borrow it for a general circuit.

The arithmetic behind the nameplate MOCP, from 440.22(A): the protective device is rated at not more than 175 percent of the compressor's rated-load current or branch-circuit selection current, whichever is greater. If a device at that rating will not carry the starting current, 440.22(A) lets the rating be increased where 175% will not carry the starting current, but not above 225%..

Worked example: a compressor with a 20 A rated-load current takes protection at 20 × 1.75 = 35 A; if 35 A will not start it, the ceiling is 20 × 2.25 = 45 A. On listed equipment the manufacturer's printed MOCP already reflects this math, so the plate still governs — this arithmetic is for the compressor-only case and for checking a plate that looks wrong. 440.22(A) also sets a floor: the device may not be less than 125 percent of the rated-load current. (440.22(B) covers equipment with more than one motor or other loads.)
sections.on_the_job: If a condenser trips a breaker sized at or below its MOCP, the fault is in the equipment or the circuit, not in the arithmetic: measure starting and running current and inspect the contactor and conductors before anyone proposes a larger breaker. A breaker above the nameplate MOCP is never the fix.

sections.title: Conductor sizing for a single motor-compressor
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 440.32 sizes conductors for a single hermetic motor-compressor:
• The conductor ampacity must be not less than 125 percent of the compressor's rated-load current, or of the branch-circuit selection current, whichever is greater.
• On listed equipment the manufacturer has already done this work and printed it as the MCA (minimum circuit ampacity) on the nameplate. The field rule and the nameplate rule agree: the conductor ampacity must be at least the MCA.
• Where you are sizing from a compressor's own data rather than a unit plate — a compressor-only replacement — this section is the arithmetic behind the plate.
Worked example: a compressor with a 20 A rated-load current needs conductors with an ampacity of at least 20 × 1.25 = 25 A, before any other checks.
sections.on_the_job: When the plate is present, wire to the MCA and do not re-derive it — on a condenser change-out, the MCA and MOCP printed on the new unit's plate are the whole sizing job. When the plate is missing or illegible on existing equipment, stop and get the data from the manufacturer rather than estimating from tonnage: a "3-ton" guess is not a current rating, and two units of the same tonnage can carry different compressors. Photograph the plate at the survey so the wire gets ordered right the first time.
sections.why_it_exists: A compressor runs for hours at a stretch through a Florida summer, and its current does not politely stop at the nameplate value on a hot roof or a low-voltage afternoon. The 125 percent margin keeps the conductors from living at their temperature limit for the whole cooling season — which is what cooks insulation, loosens terminations and starts nuisance trips that turn into callbacks.
inspection_fails: Conductors sized to the MOCP, or to a tonnage guess, instead of the nameplate MCA.
Old conductors reused on a change-out without checking them against the new unit's MCA.
Compressor-only replacement wired from the old unit's plate instead of the new compressor's rated-load or selection current.
MCA guessed from a faded, sun-bleached plate — the data was never pulled from the manufacturer.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer sizes the wire from the MOCP — or from tonnage. The MOCP is short-circuit and ground-fault protection (440.22), and it is allowed to be far larger than the conductor ampacity; it does not size the wire. Conductors come from the MCA, which is 440.32's 125 percent already worked out by the manufacturer.

sections.title: Room air conditioners (440.60–440.65)
sections.plain_explanation: Part VII of Article 440 covers the cord-and-plug room air conditioner — the window and through-wall units a tenant or homeowner plugs in. The load rules are the ones that matter: a single room unit on a branch circuit of its own may not exceed 80 percent of that circuit's rating; where the same circuit also feeds lighting or other receptacles, the unit may not exceed 50 percent. Section 440.65 adds the plug protection: single-phase room units must have leakage-current detection (LCDI) or arc-fault protection in the attachment plug or cord — the fat plug with the test buttons is a requirement, not an accessory. 440.65 also allows a factory-installed heat-detecting circuit interrupter (HDCI) besides LCDI or AFCI on single-phase cord-and-plug room air conditioners, and Part VII covers room units rated not over 40A, 250V, single-phase (440.62(A)).
sections.on_the_job: A window unit tripping a shared bedroom circuit is usually the 50 percent rule announcing itself. The fix is a dedicated circuit under the 80 percent rule, not a bigger breaker on the shared circuit.

sections.title: Generators — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 445 covers generators themselves: their marking, conductor ampacity, overcurrent protection, and shutdown controls. The working rules Sharma uses most:
• Listing: stationary generators at 600 volts or less must be listed (445.6)
• Overcurrent protection for the machine itself (445.12)
• Conductors from the generator sized at not less than 115 percent of the nameplate current rating (445.13)
• Shutdown controls, including the outdoor shutdown for a generator at a one- or two-family dwelling (445.18(D))
The transfer equipment and the optional-standby-system rules that decide what a generator may feed live mainly in Chapter 7 (Article 702), and required standby systems in 700/701 — this article is about the machine. Sharma meets 445 on whole-house generator work in dwellings, where the 2020 outdoor shutdown rule is the item inspectors ask about.
sections.on_the_job: Separate the two questions on a generator job: is the machine itself installed to 445, and is the system it feeds wired and sized to Chapter 7? Passing one does not pass the other. On a typical whole-house job the unit is a 22 kW standby generator at 240 V single-phase, nameplate current about 92 A. The feeder conductors are sized from that nameplate: 92 × 115 percent = 105.8 A, so conductors rated at least 106 A — 2 AWG copper at the 75°C column is 115 A (445.13). The shutdown device goes outside the dwelling, where occupants and first responders can reach it (445.18(D)). Cross-link to Chapter 7 for transfer-switch sizing; do not size a transfer switch from this chapter.

nec2023_change.change: A generator's disconnect can now sit inside the unit behind a hinged cover, provided a sign points to its location. The emergency shutdown rules moved out to 445.19. The disconnect can be inside the generator, behind a hinged door, cover or panel, as long as a sign meeting 110.21(B) shows where it is.

The remote shutdown switch and the dwelling shutdown device can now mount on the outside of the generator enclosure.

sections.why_it_exists: A generator is a second power source that starts by itself, often at 2 a.m. in a storm, with nobody watching. If its conductors are sized like a normal feeder, a long outage at full load overheats them. If it cannot be shut down from outside the house, first responders stand next to a running machine they cannot stop. Article 445 keeps the machine itself from becoming the emergency.
sections.exam_trap: The exam trap is sizing generator conductors at 100 percent of nameplate, like an ordinary feeder. 445.13 wants not less than 115 percent of the generator's nameplate current rating, because the machine can be asked to carry its full rating for an entire outage. A second trap: answering a transfer-switch or load question from Article 445 — what the generator may feed is decided in Chapter 7, not here.

sections.title: Stationary generators must be listed (2020 addition)
sections.plain_explanation: Section 445.6, added in the 2020 edition, requires stationary generators operating at 600 volts or less to be listed. Before this edition a generator could arrive on a job with no listing requirement stated in Article 445 itself; now the machine's listing is a code item, checked the same way as any other equipment's. The listing carries the installation instructions that 110.3(B) makes enforceable, including clearances, exhaust, and the shutdown arrangement in 445.18.
sections.on_the_job: At quote stage for a standby generator, confirm the exact model is listed and get its installation manual into the job file before the pad is poured. An unlisted or grey-market unit is a stop, not a discount. On a Sharma house job that means the quote names the exact listed model, the manual's clearance and exhaust pages go in the job file, and the outdoor shutdown arrangement (445.18) is planned from the manual — not improvised at trim-out.
sections.florida_note: Florida note: hurricane-season generator work is where unlisted units most often appear in Sharma's territory; the listing check happens at quote, not at inspection.

sections.why_it_exists: A standby generator is an engine, a fuel system and a power source in one box, installed a few feet from a house. The listing is the proof that the whole machine — not just its alternator — was evaluated as a system: fuel shutoffs, exhaust temperatures, enclosure clearances, controls. Without it, every one of those judgments lands on the installer and the inspector, one job at a time.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is the voltage line. Under the 2020 book, 445.6 reaches stationary generators at 600 volts or less — a bigger unlisted machine is outside this section's text (other rules still apply). The 2023 edition removes the limit: every stationary generator must be listed. Answering 'any voltage' on a 2020 question — or '600 volts or less' on a 2023 question — is the classic miss.

sections.title: Overcurrent protection for generators (445.12)
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 445.12 requires generators to be protected from overload:
• The protection may be inherent in the machine's design, circuit breakers, fuses, or another identified means — but one of them must be there, and it is chosen from the nameplate.
• It works with 445.13, which sizes the conductors from the generator at 115 percent of nameplate current. The generator's own protection and the wire leaving it are both chosen from the nameplate.
• A transfer scheme must never leave the generator feeding a fault or an overload with nothing able to open.
Together they mean a fault or an overload cannot cook the machine that is supposed to be the backup.
sections.on_the_job: Read the generator nameplate for both numbers at the site survey: rated amps for the 445.13 conductor math, and the machine's built-in protection for the 445.12 check. Both go on the job record. Example: a 22 kW standby unit at 240 V single-phase has a nameplate current of about 92 A, so the conductors leaving it need an ampacity of at least 92 × 1.15 = 105.8 A — call it 106 A minimum. On that same visit, confirm the unit's own breaker or inherent protection is in place before the transfer scheme is built around the machine.
sections.figure_idea: Generator nameplate card with two callouts: rated amps (wire math) and built-in protection (overload check).
sections.why_it_exists: During an outage the generator is the only source the building has, and it will try to feed whatever is connected — including a fault — until something opens or something burns. A generator's windings are not sized to carry fault or overload current while it waits for help. Overload protection at the machine is what lets the backup survive the emergency it was bought for.
inspection_fails: Generator installed with no inherent overload protection and no breaker or fuses at the machine.
Conductors from the generator sized at 100 percent of nameplate instead of the 115 percent 445.13 requires.
Nameplate rated amps never recorded at the survey, so the conductor math and the protection check were both guessed.
Transfer arrangement leaves the generator able to feed a fault with no device able to open.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is "the feeder breaker in the panel protects the generator, so the machine needs nothing of its own." 445.12 puts the overload protection on the generator itself — inherent design, its own breakers or fuses, or another identified means. A downstream panel breaker is distribution protection; it is not the machine's overload protection.

sections.title: Generator conductors — 115 percent of nameplate current
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 445.13 sizes the conductors from a generator to its first distribution device or devices at not less than 115 percent of the generator's nameplate current rating, with the article's own provisions for cases where design prevents overloading. The margin exists because a generator can be asked to carry its full rating for the whole duration of an outage. Neutral conductor treatment has its own paragraphs in this section, so do not assume the neutral is automatically the same size as the ungrounded conductors on every system type.

Worked example: a 22 kW standby unit at 240 V single-phase has a nameplate current of about 92 A; 92 × 1.15 = 105.8 A minimum conductor ampacity — the feeder lands on conductors rated at least 106 A (2 AWG copper at the 75°C column is 115 A), with the overcurrent arrangement set by the generator and transfer equipment design.
sections.on_the_job: Size from the nameplate on the actual machine, and confirm whether the installation is a separately derived system before you settle the neutral and grounding arrangement — that decision belongs with the Chapter 2/Chapter 7 pages and the transfer equipment, and it changes this section's wiring.

sections.title: Outdoor shutdown for a generator at a one-family dwelling
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 445.18(D) is the 2020 provision the brief assigns to the emergency shutdown of a generator installed outdoors at a one- or two-family dwelling: in addition to the shutdown provisions that apply to generators generally, a dwelling unit generator located outside must have a readily accessible disconnecting/shutdown device located outside the dwelling, so the machine can be shut down by occupants or first responders without entering the building or standing at the machine itself. Read it together with the rest of 445.18, which governs shutdown of the prime mover generally.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 445.19: The emergency-shutdown rules moved from 445.18 to new 445.19; for one- and two-family dwellings the remote emergency shutdown must be outside the dwelling (445.19(C)). 445.18 now lets the generator disconnect sit inside the unit behind a cover if a 110.21(B) sign shows where it is.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: On a dwelling generator job, locate the outdoor shutdown where a responder would look for it — at the normal entry side of the house, plainly identified — and test it at start-up. Confirm the device you installed is the one the generator's listing and the AHJ expect; note its location on the job record and the panel directory.

sections.title: Transformers and transformer vaults — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 450 covers transformers: overcurrent protection of the transformer and its conductors, location, guarding, ventilation, and the vault construction rules for indoor installations. Sharma's day-to-day contact is the small dry-type transformer in light commercial work — a 480-to-208/120 step-down or a control transformer — where the protection table and the primary/secondary conductor rules are the working content. Vault and liquid-filled rules are later-pass material for this book.
• Protection comes from the 450.3 tables — Table 450.3(B) for transformers at 1000 V and below. The answer depends on the transformer's rated currents and on whether protection is primary-only or on both sides; never carry one remembered percentage to a different case.
• Location has teeth: an indoor dry-type of 112½ kVA or less sits at least 12 in. from combustible material, unless a fire-resistant, heat-insulating barrier separates them (450.21). Larger indoor dry-types go in a transformer room of fire-resistant construction.
• Ventilation is an installation requirement, not housekeeping (450.9): air must circulate and carry the heat away, and the vents stay clear.
sections.on_the_job: For a dry-type install: confirm primary and secondary protection against the 450.3 table for the actual voltages, confirm the secondary conductors are protected as Chapter 2 requires, and keep ventilation clearances the listing demands. Photograph the transformer nameplate into the job file. Worked example from the 450.3 page: a 45 kVA, 480-to-208/120 V dry-type draws about 54 A on the primary, so primary-only protection at 125 percent is 67.5 A and a 70 A device is the standard pick. Set the unit with its 12 in. of air off the combustible wall, vents open top and bottom.

sections.why_it_exists: A transformer is a heater that also changes voltage — its losses come out as heat, and its failure mode is insulation cooking slowly until a winding shorts. The protection table balances two jobs: small enough to clear a faulted winding, large enough to ride through magnetizing inrush every time the primary is energized. The clearance and ventilation rules keep the transformer's steady heat away from things that burn.

sections.title: Overcurrent protection for transformers
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 450.3 sets transformer overcurrent protection through its tables, one for transformers over 1000V and one for 1000V and below, with the required protection depending on voltage, whether protection is primary-only or primary-and-secondary, and the transformer's impedance where the table calls for it. Primary-only protection is permitted only within the table's limits; beyond them, both sides must be protected. The percentages are table lookups for the specific case — do not carry one remembered percentage to a different voltage or impedance.

The Table 450.3(B) rows (1000 V and below) that cover the dry-type work Sharma actually sets:
• Primary and secondary currents of 9 A or more, primary protection only — 125 percent of rated primary current
• Same size range, protection on both sides — primary up to 250 percent, secondary not over 125 percent
• Primary current under 9 A, primary protection only — up to 167 percent
• Primary current under 2 A, primary protection only — up to 300 percent
Where the calculated percentage falls between standard device ratings, the table's notes permit the next higher standard rating in the cases they cover.

Worked example: a 45 kVA, 480-to-208/120 V transformer draws about 54 A on the primary; primary-only protection is 54 × 1.25 = 67.5 A, so a 70 A device is the standard pick.
sections.on_the_job: Work the table for the case in front of you and write the case (voltage class, impedance, primary-only or both) on the worksheet. If the impedance is not on the nameplate you can read, stop — the table answer may depend on it.

sections.title: Transformer ventilation — and no storage on top
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 450.9 requires a transformer to be installed so air can circulate and carry its heat away. Ventilation is an installation requirement, not a housekeeping preference.
• Keep every vent opening clear — no stored material against the vented faces, and no wall, cover, or other equipment set so close that it chokes the airflow the manufacturer designed for.
• The horizontal top surface of a covered dry-type transformer is marked against use for storage. Treat the top as equipment space, never as a shelf.
• A transformer is a heater by design losses. Even idling it warms up; under load the heat has to leave, or the winding temperature climbs and the insulation ages fast.
Heat leaving the unit is only half the location check. Section 450.21 covers keeping that heat away from combustible material: 12 in of separation for dry-types rated 112½ kVA or less, unless a fire-resistant, heat-insulating barrier separates them.
sections.on_the_job: On a service call at a Winter Park strip center, Sharma found a 45 kVA, 480-to-208/120 V dry-type — the size the shop sets most — with paint cans and spare ceiling tiles stacked on its top and boxes of lamps tight against both vented sides. The case was hot to the touch and the unit was humming hard. The crew cleared the top and the vents, confirmed the 12 in to the wood-framed closet wall (450.21), and photographed the storage for the job report rather than just moving it quietly — storage moved without a word is back within a month.
sections.why_it_exists: Insulation life is a temperature story. A dry-type transformer that cannot shed heat runs its windings hotter every loaded hour, and the insulation breaks down years early — brittle leads and heat damage first, and in the worst case a fault inside a sealed case in an occupied building. Blocked vents and storage on top trip nothing and alarm nothing; they just cook the unit quietly until it fails.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating the flat top of a dry-type transformer as dead space: 'It is only storage — the transformer still runs.' The top of a covered dry-type is marked against storage, and blocking the unit's heat path is an installation failure whether or not anything has failed yet. The second trap is calling ventilation the manufacturer's problem. Section 450.9 puts it on the installer.

sections.title: A transformer needs a disconnecting means
sections.plain_explanation: Section 450.14 requires a disconnecting means for transformers, located either in a readily accessible location within sight of the transformer or in a remote location, with the article's exceptions (which include certain small transformers such as Class 2 and similar limited cases). Where the disconnect is remote, it must be lockable in the open position and the transformer must be marked with the disconnect's location, so a person servicing the transformer can find and secure its source. The 2020 clarifications to this section are about exactly that remote case.
sections.on_the_job: On a dry-type install, decide the disconnect location with the transformer location, not after. If the disconnect ends up remote, apply the lockable arrangement and the location marking in the same visit and record both in the job file.

sections.title: Where dry-type transformers may sit (450.21)
sections.plain_explanation: Section 450.21 governs indoor dry-type transformer locations. Transformers rated 112½ kVA or less must sit at least 12 inches from combustible material, unless separated from it by a fire-resistant, heat-insulating barrier. This does not apply to transformers rated 1000V or less that are completely enclosed, except for ventilating openings (450.21(A) Exception). Larger indoor dry-types — over 112½ kVA — go in a transformer room of fire-resistant construction with a minimum 1-hour fire rating, with the section's exceptions: Exception No. 1 covers Class 155 or higher insulation systems separated by a fire-resistant, heat-insulating barrier, or by at least 6 ft horizontally and 12 ft vertically from combustible material. Ventilation under 450.9 keeps the heat moving; this section keeps the heat away from things that burn.
sections.on_the_job: Setting a dry-type in a wood-framed electrical closet: measure the 12 inches before the transformer is hung, not after. The closet's wall finish decides which rule you are under — confirm what the wall is made of.

sections.title: Phase converters — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 455 covers phase converters, the equipment that lets three-phase motors run from a single-phase supply.
• Two kinds (455.2): rotary converters, which make the third phase with a rotating idler, and static converters, which do it with capacitors and electronics.
• Marking (455.4): the nameplate states the maker, input and output voltages, frequency, rated single-phase input full-load amperes, and the minimum, maximum single, and total load the converter may serve.
• Supply conductors (455.6(A)(1)): for variable loads, ampacity at least 125 percent of the nameplate single-phase input full-load amperes.
• Overcurrent protection (455.7): not over 125 percent of the rated input current.
• Disconnect (455.8): in sight of the converter, rated at least 115 percent of the nameplate input amperes.
• The manufactured phase (455.6(B), 455.9): the leg the converter creates gets a distinctive marking everywhere it is accessible, and no single-phase load is connected to it.
Sizing throughout the article is tied to the converter and the largest motor or load it serves. Sharma meets converters rarely, on small commercial and agricultural-type jobs at the edge of its territory; this page gives the article its place and scope.
sections.on_the_job: A converter is sized to its load, not to the building service. Get the motor data for everything the converter will ever run at once, and give that list to the office before quoting the install. Worked example: a small shop's rotary converter is nameplated 40 A single-phase input. The supply conductors need at least 125 percent of 40 A, so 50 A ampacity (8 AWG copper). The breaker may not exceed 125 percent, so 50 A. The disconnect must be at least 115 percent, which is 46 A, so a 60 A switch goes in, in sight of the converter.
sections.why_it_exists: A converter is a motor load with heavy starting current, and its nameplate input is the only honest measure of what the supply will see. Undersize the input and the three-phase motors start hard, run hot and trip. The manufactured leg is its own hazard: it is not a utility phase, and a 120 V load landed on it can be damaged, or damage the balance of the system.
inspection_fails: Supply conductors sized to the motor load instead of 125 percent of the converter nameplate input.
Manufactured phase not identified: no distinctive marking where the conductors are accessible.
Single-phase load connected to the manufactured phase.
No disconnect in sight of the converter, or one rated under 115 percent of the nameplate input.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing the supply from the three-phase motor's full-load amps, the way a normal motor feeder is figured. Article 455 keys everything to the converter's nameplate single-phase input: conductors at 125 percent of that number, not of the motor's.

sections.title: Capacitors — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 460 covers capacitors installed on electrical systems, most often for power-factor correction on commercial services and large motor loads.
• Conductors are sized above the capacitor's rated current: ampacity not less than 135 percent of rated current (460.8(A)). Conductors tying a capacitor into a motor circuit are also at least one-third the ampacity of the motor circuit conductors.
• Overcurrent protection and a disconnecting means are part of every capacitor installation, and the disconnect is rated not less than 135 percent of rated current (460.8).
• A capacitor holds its charge after it is switched off. A discharge means must bring the residual voltage down to 50 volts or less within 1 minute after disconnection; equipment over 1000 volts gets 5 minutes (460.6).
• Capacitor cases are grounded (460.10), and every capacitor carries a nameplate giving the manufacturer, rated voltage, frequency, kvar or amperes, number of phases, and whether it has an internal discharge device (460.12).
That stored charge is the safety point of the article: a disconnected capacitor is not automatically a dead capacitor.
sections.on_the_job: On a power-factor correction job at a small commercial service, the bank's nameplate reads 60 A rated current. The conductors are sized at 135 percent — 81 A ampacity minimum — before the run is pulled. Treat capacitor terminals as live until discharged and verified with a meter. Allow the discharge device its time, then test — never assume. Include the capacitor's kvar and voltage from its nameplate in the job record.
sections.why_it_exists: A capacitor is a battery that charges in a fraction of a second. Open the disconnect and the bank can sit at full voltage, waiting for the next pair of hands. The discharge rule exists so the stored energy bleeds off on a timer instead of through a person. The 135 percent conductor rule exists because a capacitor circuit runs hotter than its nameplate suggests once harmonics and tolerance stack up in service.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'the capacitor is dead once the disconnect is open.' It is not: it holds its charge until the discharge means bleeds it down, and 460.6 allows a full minute to get to 50 volts. Test before touch, every time. Second trap: sizing the conductors at 100 percent of rated current — capacitor circuits take 135 percent (460.8(A)).
